Rascal Does Not Dream of a Beach Queen, Vol. 16

One day, Sakuta Azusagawa met a girl in the men’s room.

Rascal Does Not Dream of a Beach Queen, Vol. 16

Rascal Does Not Dream of a Beach Queen, Vol. 16

1

“Good morning!”

A familiar voice cut through his slumber. It didn’t take long for him to place it—his sister, Kaede.

“Time to rise and shine, Sakuta!”

She was shaking him.

“If you don’t get up real soon, I’ll have to sleep with you!”

That sounded a bit too eager, which convinced him to finally start moving.

“Then I’d better get out of bed.”

He sat up.

“Aw, already?”

Kaede was ostensibly here to wake him but sounded disappointed. She lowered her leg back to the ground.

“Well, this was your idea.”

“This was supposed to be a special bonus round that would let me legally sneak into your bed! Where’d it go?!”

“Somewhere other than here.”

He wasn’t sure where and was even less sure he cared.

“Morning, Kaede.”

It was that time of day.

“Good morning, Sakuta!” Kaede exclaimed with a huge smile.

Sakuta answered with a yawn, then stretched and sighed.

“What time is it?” he asked, turning to the clock.

“It’s seven AM!” Kaede said, getting there first. The clock confirmed her words.

It was October 5. Sunday. In other words—a day off.

“Good night,” Sakuta said, toppling back over. He closed his eyes, prepared to plunge back into dreams.

“Y-you can’t, Sakuta!”

Kaede wasn’t letting him.

She was shaking him even harder than before.

“You said you have the sports festival today! Festival fever! Wasshoi!”

That did ring a bell. He may have said something last night.

October 5. His school’s sports festival. He remembered grumbling that it wasn’t even Sports Day (October 13).

Seeing no other choice, he got up again.

“Uh, Kaede.”

“Yes?”

“What do you know about sports festivals?”

“That’s the day the broadcast club says, ‘Go, red team!’ even though they clearly don’t care!”

“Exactly. I’m impressed.”

That one line said everything.

“You told me that yesterday!”

“Did I?”

“You did. I remember everything you say to me!”

Kaede puffed herself up with pride. She puffed herself up so much she started coughing. Sakuta patted her back, then dragged himself out of bed.

Apparently, he had to go to school.

2

“Let the Minegahara High Sports Festival begin!”

The admin committee member’s cry was met with a roar. There were boys yelling “Sports festival time!” like they’d been waiting their whole lives for this. Some of them were just bellowing incoherently. One dude put his fingers in his mouth, whistling; quite a lot of girls were squealing. The noise level on the Minegahara grounds was far too high for the early hour.

The entire student body had assembled outside. Nine classes in each year, nearly a thousand students in all. They’d been split into three color camps—red, blue, and yellow—and were standing in their respective color’s assigned section of the grounds.

The red team had a cheer squad leading them in a “We! Will! Win!” chant. The blue team was fighting back with “Blue! Team! Victory!” and the yellow team wasn’t exactly staying quiet. A group of girls were getting a “Yellow! Let’s go!” chant going.

Ripples ran across the tricolored mob. Spirits clashed beneath clear fall skies.

This excitement came only once a year—but Sakuta was just standing at the back of the blue crowd, watching with listless eyes. He was hardly alone.

Maybe half the student body were really into this. Another 30 percent were halfheartedly going along with it. The remaining 20 percent weren’t feeling it at all and, like Sakuta, were doing their best to get out from underfoot. This was equally true for the red and yellow teams.

Some people like sports festivals; some people don’t. Sakuta had never been one to go with the crowd, and anywhere you went, there were people like him. This was true for all high schools, yet they all had sports festivals anyway.

“The first event is the Moving Ball Toss! Team reps, assemble at the entrance!”

The admin committee announcement came from a tent set up by the school building. The noise finally started dying down. Each team started getting ready for the games.

People were restlessly shifting from right to left, and from left to right.

It was unbelievable how motivated everyone was. They were so vibrant and dazzling that Sakuta couldn’t bear to look. He yawned instead.

“Azusagawa,” someone said. “What are you in for?”

He turned to find one of his few friends—Rio Futaba.

“……”

It took him a moment to answer—his eyes got caught on her outfit. She never dressed like this, and it distracted him.

“No white coat,” he mumbled.

“Obviously.”

She was wearing the school tracksuit. When he looked her up and down, Rio shot him a look of undisguised disgust.

The tracksuit was a little baggy, probably an attempt to obfuscate her figure. Primarily to avoid getting stares from the boys, most likely.

She had her hair up, so he could see the pale nape of her neck peeping out of the collar. Weirdly sexy. Like Sakuta, she was wearing a blue headband. Today, they were teammates.

Clothing aside, there was one other big difference—Rio wasn’t wearing glasses. That reminded him of the other Rio—from when she’d split in two.

She must have noticed because she said, “I haven’t split again. I’m just wearing contacts since they’re gonna make me run.”

The look on her face made it clear she was not pleased about this.

“When are you up, Futaba?”

“We pulled lots, and I got stuck with the scavenger race.”

She sounded deeply depressed about it. He assumed that was genuine. Sports or not, Rio absolutely loathed doing anything in public.

“You?” she asked.

“I’m the alternate, so I’m just watching.”

Sakuta’s class had divvied up the events based on who wanted to be in them. If he didn’t want to be in anything, he didn’t have to. But they had to maintain appearances, so he’d been entered as a backup.

“I hope lots of people are sick.”

“Don’t jinx me.”

Saying these things out loud could make them come true. That was how the world worked.

“Is Sakurajima here today?”

“Nope.”

“Because of the media circus?”

“More or less. She talked to the school, and they excused her from the festival—too many outside visitors.”

Mai had called to tell him yesterday.

Since the press conference, the buzz was steadily dying down, but it was the first time the famous Mai Sakurajima had ever courted anything approaching controversy, and it was still a pretty hot topic. Student families and alumni regularly attended the sports festival, so the school wasn’t inclined to stir the pot.

Mai didn’t care for unwanted attention. And Sakuta would never make her do anything she didn’t like. Even if she was a third-year and this would be their last chance to be in a sports festival together.

Also, he knew half the reason she wasn’t coming was for his benefit. He was the one who’d had his photo in the weekly magazines next to her.

For the time being, they were avoiding being seen together—even in the halls at school. Sakuta was already getting plenty of glances on his own; when he was with Mai, they’d have every eye on them.

When would the world let him flirt with her again? Not anytime soon, as far as he could tell.

“So that’s why you seem more lifeless than usual.”

“Why am I even at school if Mai’s not here?”

“For the sports festival, clearly,” Rio said, exasperated. With that, she headed toward the building.

“Where are you going, Futaba?!”

“I’ve got time before my event, so I’m gonna make some coffee in the lab,” she said, pausing.

“Sounds great. I’m coming, too.”

“I think you’re needed elsewhere, Azusagawa.”

“Huh?”

He had no clue what she meant.

“Kunimi’s calling for you,” Rio said, looking over his shoulder.

Apparently, someone behind him. Probably Yuuma Kunimi.

Sakuta turned around.

“Sakuta! Over here!” Yuuma was waving to him from the Ball Toss group. No—that was a beckon.

“You come to me,” he grumbled. Yuuma likely hadn’t heard him but came jogging over anyway, accompanied by a petite schoolgirl with a basket on her back.

Tomoe Koga, a first-year.

She had the same blue headband as Yuuma and Sakuta. She looked a bit different. Most likely because her fluffy short hair was braided above the ears.

Their eyes met, and she immediately said, “It gets messed up when I run.”

He hadn’t even said anything, but she was still sulking about it.

“It’s not like I’m super excited about the festival or anything.”

He had no idea who she was making excuses for, but Tomoe’s life sure seemed filled with hardship.

“Well, I think it’s cute.”

“D-don’t call me cute.”

“Then…mega-cute?”

“You are so annoying!”

Tomoe puffed out her cheeks in protest, so he turned back toward Yuuma.

“So what do you want?”

“We’ve got a no-show for the ball toss, so you’ll need to step in.”

“Seriously?”

“Yeppp.”

The very first event. Unbelievable. Rio had totally jinxed him. And she’d already ditched him for the science lab.

“Who the hell had the nerve?”

“Ootsu, from my class,” Yuuma said.

Sakuta didn’t recognize the name.

“Who?”

“Ootsu. Minagi Ootsu.”

Yuuma seemed certain he would know who that was.

“She was in class when we took attendance this morning, so she’s not out sick, but we can’t find her.”

“I dunno who she is, but I’m holding this against her.”

“Huh? Senpai, you seriously don’t know her?”

Tomoe stared at him in disbelief.

“Ootsu who? Never heard of her. For all I know, she just hates sports and is hiding in a bathroom stall.”

“Koga already searched those,” Yuuma said.

“Yeah,” Tomoe confirmed with a nod.

“And Ootsu’s the last person to hate sports.”

Yuuma seemed weirdly sure of that.

“Why are you so confident?”

“How do you not know?” Tomoe asked, genuinely appalled.

“I just don’t, okay? What, is Ootsu famous like Mai?”

“Not quite that famous, but close.”

Yuuma was wincing a bit, too. Maybe Tomoe was right and everyone else knew the name.

“But Senpai’s a caveman who doesn’t own a phone,” Tomoe said, mostly to herself. “At our school, Sakurajima’s the only one more famous than her.”

“Huh.”

That didn’t mean much to Sakuta.

“Look here,” Tomoe said, shoving a phone in his face.

“It’s the sports festival. Leave your phone in your locker…”

“I’m taking pictures with it! And it’s not just me!”

He looked around and did see several other students carrying phones. Groups of friends taking pictures of each other…clearly having fun.

“Look at the screen!”

He did as he was told, turning his gaze toward the phone Tomoe was holding up for him. It had a picture of a tanned girl in a swimsuit. Her sporty bikini showed off her athletic build.

She was smiling beneath a clear blue sky. Her white teeth gleamed. One strap of her top was out of place, showing a tan line beneath it that also gleamed.

Her feet were in the sand. A net stretched between two poles behind her—he also spotted a brightly colored volleyball.

That was enough clues to tell him that this Minagi Ootsu must play beach volleyball.

“I do like tans,” he said, offering his honest opinion of the photo.

Sakuta’s girlfriend, Mai, refused to let herself tan at all, so this was a nice change of pace. His interest rose a tiny bit.

The grass is always greener.

“Senpai, don’t leer.”

Tomoe was giving him a look of utter contempt.

“Don’t worry, Koga.”

“About what?”

“What’s inside my head is even worse.”

“Senpai…you’re the worst.”

Maybe he’d pushed his luck. She sounded like she meant it.

“So, this is Ootsu…Minagi, was it?”

“Yeah, she’s a junior athlete. Plays beach volleyball. She got picked for the youth Olympics, and they’ve done profiles of her on TV.”

Yuuma gave him a searching look to see if that rang any bells, but Sakuta just shook his head. She hadn’t crossed his radar at all.

“Senpai, do you, like, not watch TV?”

“That’s for watching Mai.”

“Maybe at your house,” Yuuma said, chuckling. “But like I said, Ootsu’s an athlete. And she has zero problems being in front of crowds. I doubt she’s gotten stage fright about the sports festival.”

The info they’d provided almost certainly ruled out that possibility. If anything, she seemed like the type who’d get all excited about the idea. And the crowds wouldn’t faze her.

But it was hardly the time to stand around discussing her motives.

“So you’re down a member?”

That fact wasn’t changing.

“Yep.”

“Then someone’ll have to step in.”

“I’m glad you’re with us.”

Yuuma clapped his hands on Sakuta’s shoulders. He considered running, but Yuuma was well built and did not seem inclined to let go.

“Kunimi, who’ll carry the basket? That was supposed to be Ootsu.”

Tomoe held up the basket in question. This was “Moving” Ball Toss, so each team had one player carrying a basket on their back. The opposing teams would chase that player around, tossing balls into their basket. A three-way struggle between the red, blue, and yellow teams.

“Blue team, start positions! Be here in one minute or you’re disqualified!”

An announcement came from the admin booth.

The red and yellow teams were already in place on the east and west sides of the grounds, waiting for the blue team to arrive at the north end.

“Koga, gimme that,” he said, taking the basket off her.

“Huh? You’re gonna carry it?”

Tomoe looked surprised. Even more so when he put the basket on her.

“Wuh?”

“Good to go.”

“Wait, no, Senpai! I can’t! I’m the worst choice ever!” she cried, looking like she was about to burst into tears.

“Trust me, Koga. With a fragile little thing like you on basket duty, no one’ll want to throw balls your way. Especially the boys.”

Nobody would want to chase down a cute girl and throw balls at her as hard as they could when the whole school was watching. Even the boys all fired up about the sports festival were mostly just hoping it would help them score with the girls. Winning the Ball Toss was simply not worth getting yourself branded as a monster who’d go all out and pick on a girl. Imagine spending the rest of high school as the asshole who hit a girl with a ball… It was basic psychology.

“He’s got a point,” Yuuma said, nodding.

“You too?!”

“Well, we’ll cover you. Here, Sakuta, this one’s yours.”

Yuuma handed him a giant…fan? Maybe a yard across. The idea must be to block balls thrown at Tomoe’s basket, knocking them out of the air.

“S-Senpai, you’d better keep me safe!” Tomoe wailed, looking very nervous.

“Kunimi, you’d better keep me safe,” Sakuta said.

“What do you even mean?”

Tomoe looked tense, Sakuta unmotivated—but Yuuma alone seemed ready to have some fun.

3

“One, two, three!”

The crowd joined the chanting as red, blue, and yellow balls hurtled through the air. All three were thrown by three students wearing admin committee armbands.

“Four, five, six!”

Each new number got a whoop from the audience. They must have known that the outcome would never be decided this early, but…the rush of the sports festival had everyone fired up.

It was better to have fun with it. Part of Sakuta envied people who could get worked up about these things.

He was keeping his distance from that vibe, sitting with his back against one of the soccer goalposts.

Maybe collapsed was a more accurate word.

He didn’t have it in him to lift his head, much less keep track of the score. It didn’t matter if they won. He’d been running flat out the whole event and was dead tired. He didn’t even want to think. He might be up for a drink of water, though.

“Sakuta, you alive?”

A shadow crossed his vision. He didn’t have to look up to know that it was Kunimi. Even his voice was pleasantly handsome.

“Yo, Kunimi.”

“What?”

“Let’s tell the admin committee to change the name from Ball Toss to Ball Barrage.”

He barely managed to get the words out. His voice was a hoarse rasp.

“You sound fine.”

Sakuta had no clue what could have possibly led to that conclusion, but Yuuma was smiling and nodding. They’d both been in the same event, so why was Yuuma still full of life while Sakuta felt like he’d been put through the wringer?

Putting the basket on a timid-looking girl to dampen their opponents’ aggression—that tactic had paid off.

Seconds after the starting gun, both red and yellow team members had held back. Tomoe was so obviously spooked it made their hearts waver.

It had been especially effective against the male opponents. Instead of charging out, they simply exchanged glances and checked what the other boys were doing.

The blue team seized this golden opportunity to go after the red basket.

The star of the men’s track team was carrying the red team basket and was fast on his feet, but the yellow team quickly joined the attack and helped surround him, filling his basket fast.

No matter how excellent a sprinter, he didn’t stand a chance once the basket on his back got heavier and heavier.

The rest of red team was in disarray, so early on, all Sakuta had to do was keep up with Tomoe, who kept screaming “They’re here, they’re here, Senpai, help!” the whole time. But only early on.

Tomoe was invincible where the boys were concerned, but from the middle of the game, a group of sports club girls got organized and made a concerted effort to hurl balls at her from all directions. They didn’t let up until the end of the match.

And since Tomoe was hiding behind Sakuta as much as she could, most of the balls hit him instead. Hit him, crashed into him, smacked him around… The barrage was relentless.

He tried blocking with that oversized fan, but it was made of cardboard and broke right away. No use at all.

His body took the brunt of it.

You could still see the imprints of the balls on his tracksuit. He was battered all over. What part of this raggedy man was “fine”?

Sakuta caught his breath and finally looked up.

“You aren’t even dirty. How is that possible?”

Yuuma’s tracksuit might as well have been fresh out of the laundry. Not a single ball mark on it.

“I just dodged or used the fan.”

“Casually bragging about how athletic you are? I hate you.”

“And they didn’t come after me as bad.”

“Mm?”

“Sakuta, you do realize a healthy chunk of those dudes were aiming for you specifically, right?”

“I was hoping that was my imagination.”

He’d had a hunch that was the case. No, that was a lie. He’d known more or less right away. Several of those dudes clearly had it in for him.

“The least they could do is try to hide it. Are they that jealous that I’m with Mai?” Sakuta asked, getting right to the cause.

“Well, yeah, why wouldn’t they be?” Yuuma cackled.

What an aggravating laugh. His irritation didn’t last long—because there was something else Sakuta had noticed in the thick of the action.

Every time someone came after Sakuta, Yuuma had struck back—with a much harder throw. While also protecting Tomoe from the onslaught. If he was capable of all that, perhaps he could have tried to defend Sakuta a little, too…but that was how Yuuma Kunimi did things.

Sakuta was breathing normally again, so he got up.

“Oh, Senpai, there you are.”

Tomoe came running over to them.

“Are you okay?” she asked, peering up at his face.

“Do I look okay?”

He spread his arms out, waving at the marks on his tracksuit.

“You’ve got chalk on your face,” Tomoe said, giggling.

“Oh, Koga, you’ve got marks on your butt.”

“Eek! I do?” She twisted herself, trying to see. “Where?”

“Should I dust them off for you?”

“Oh, okay… No, do not do that!”

She guarded her butt with both hands.

“Don’t be shy.”

“I’m not being shy!”

“I think nothing of touching your butt.”

“I don’t want you to!”

Tomoe slapped her own butt, fuming the whole time. She soon got it clean. Sakuta would not need to help after all.

“You two are close as always,” Yuuma said, watching them bicker.

“Well, we kicked each other’s butts once.”

“Will you stop telling people that?!”

“Oh, they’re almost finished.”

Ignoring Tomoe’s protests, Sakuta shifted his attention to the center of the grounds.

The red team’s loss was already set in stone, so now it was just blue and yellow in the running.

“Fifty-one. Fifty-two…… Ah! No more yellow balls! Blue team wins the Moving Ball Toss!”

The blue-team stands exploded.

“Woo-hoo! We did it, Senpai!” Tomoe was jumping for joy. “Thank goodness—I didn’t want anyone blaming me for the loss…,” she muttered, relieved.

Sakuta turned his back on that and headed toward the school building.

“Oh, Senpai! Where you going?”

“Gonna wash my face.”

He had dirt in his mouth.

He also planned to take a breather in a classroom somewhere, but he didn’t tell her that.

4

In a dramatic departure from the schoolyard, an eerie hush had fallen over the hallways and classrooms. Every now and then, a cheer or wail would pierce the silence, but the farther into the building he got, the fainter those grew. Like they drifted over from some far-off world.

The only sound close at hand was his soles scraping the floor.

Sakuta went upstairs to the second story, and the sounds grew even fainter. Perfect for a nap.

Before heading to his classroom, he ducked into the men’s room to wash his face and rinse out his mouth. At the sink, he found a raggedy boy looking back at him. Tragically, this was his own reflection.

First, he washed the dirt off his face. There was chalk dust in his hair, so he spot cleaned that, checking his progress against the mirror. He took the tracksuit off completely and shook the dirt off out the window. Then he put it back on and took a leak while he was there.

“Whew.”

Feeling much better, he put his underwear and tracksuit pants back where they belonged. Now all he had to do was go back to class for a nice long nap. When he woke up, he’d probably hit up the science lab for some instant coffee.

That was Sakuta’s original plan, but even after washing his hands, he didn’t head to the classroom. He didn’t even take a step toward the exit.

Something felt off.

And had since he stepped in here.

The source of this came from the third stall, at the far back.

The only stall with a closed door.

The only one in use.

The entire time Sakuta had been cleaning himself up, there’d been another student here. Sitting there inside the toilet stall—and yet they had not made a single sound.

No grunts, no toilet paper unrolling, no flushes.

The silence behind that door was unnatural, intentionally stifled.

An artificial hush.

Sakuta was confident that silence proved there was someone in the stall. Ironically.

It bugged him.

Bugged him enough to notice…

…that there was a faint fragrance in the air. A pleasant scent ill-suited for the men’s room.

If this hadn’t been the day of the sports festival, he’d have moved right along. If he hadn’t just heard about a missing female student, he’d have left the bathroom without a second thought. That was the normal thing to do.

But he remembered that Tomoe had already checked the ladies’ rooms.

And he was pretty sure she hadn’t checked the men’s rooms.

No one would go searching for a girl in the men’s room. That was the last place anyone would look.

Which made them excellent hiding places.

Sakuta moved to the closed stall door. Part of him was trying to convince himself he was wrong, but he knocked twice anyway.

“……”

He waited but got no answer.

The silence of a held breath. Whoever was in there was probably focusing entirely on their ears, listening to the sounds outside—to the sounds Sakuta made.

“If I’m wrong, you don’t have to answer,” he said, ignoring these efforts. “But is that you, Ootsu?”

He had asked the big question. It was the most plausible explanation for this.

“……”

Still no answer. No answer, but there was a noise. A squeak of slippers on the floor.

That was all the reaction he got.

“……”

Sakuta was certain now someone was in there, but they weren’t talking.

“Sorry, guess I was wrong. Didn’t mean to interrupt. I’ll be going now, so take your time.”

Sakuta wasn’t into chatting up empty stalls, so he turned to go.

He made it three steps away before he heard a metallic clank behind him. Then came the creak of hinges…

Sakuta turned back to find the stall door cracked open. He could tell someone was peering out of it.

Their eyes met, but the crack was too small for him to make out their face. When he squinted, they pulled back out of sight.

Instead, a hand extended, beckoning to him.

A very surreal image. Like something from a horror film. What was the bathroom ghost called? Hanako? He wasn’t exactly an expert.

It was still beckoning.

“What, you gonna give me something?”

This smelled like trouble, but he headed over anyway.

“I’m here,” he said, stopping outside the door.

A second later, the hand reached out and grabbed him by the wrist. Then it pulled, hard.

“Uh, hey! What? Why?!” he spluttered.

Oblivious to Sakuta’s consternation, the toilet hand was pulling him into the stall.

“Wait, hang on! We can work this out! Just let me go!” he wailed.

“No, I can’t let you go! You have to stay!”

A girl’s voice came from behind the door. On closer inspection, the hand on his wrist seemed rather feminine as well. A bit large for a girl, but the nails were painted a very cute color.

“Words are hard…”

Sakuta had been misunderstood so badly that he went limp from resignation, and was promptly dragged into the stall. The lingering fatigue of the Ball Toss meant he lacked the strength to resist much anyway.

The door slammed shut and the latch slid home.

Sakuta had been captured.

Now he was all alone in a bathroom stall with a mystery girl.

What in the world was going on?

“……”

“……”

Honestly, he wanted to be anywhere else. But the girl had his hands pinned in front of him like he was under arrest, and escape was not an option.

On the other hand, they were facing each other, and he finally got a good look at the stall’s occupant.

She was the same height as Mai or slightly taller. Probably almost five foot seven. Short hair, neatly trimmed above the shoulders. It was October, but she still had a striking tan. And he had seen the girl’s face before.

She was the spitting image of the photo Tomoe had shown him just before the Moving Ball Toss match. This was clearly Minagi Ootsu, the girl everyone had been searching for without success.

She was wearing a tracksuit. Even beach volleyball stars didn’t spend all their time in bikinis. Obviously.

“Can you at least let go of my hand?” Sakuta asked, when she didn’t speak.

“And give you a chance to escape, Azusagawa?”

“Mm? You know who I am?”

He had not expected her to know his name.

“Of course I do. You’re famous.”

Probably not for any good reasons. It had to be the hospitalization incident, or recklessly asking Mai out in front of the whole school…one or the other.

“I think you’re the famous one, Ootsu. Because of the whole beach volleyball thing.”

“We’re the same age. No need to treat me like I’m special.”

“Okay, Ootsu, I have some words for you.”

“What?”

“No matter how kinky you are, I won’t tell anyone, so can I have my hand back now?”

“I’m hiding in the men’s room because I knew they’d search the ladies’ rooms. Not because I’m into peeping or anything.”

Minagi clearly wanted to make it clear that no kinks were involved. But she was in the men’s room. Even if he didn’t intend to peep, if Sakuta went in the ladies’ room, he’d be in hot water. The world clearly wasn’t ready for true gender equality yet.

“Let’s put the kinkiness of it aside for now, because frankly, I don’t care why you’re hiding in the bathroom, Ootsu. And I promise I won’t tell anyone where you are. So could you let go now?”

“I’ve never spoken to you before, Azusagawa. I find you hard to trust.”

“Do these look like the eyes of a liar?”

“They look like the eyes of the mackerel I had for breakfast.”

“And have you ever been betrayed by a dried fish?”

Buy ’em, fry ’em, eat ’em. No need to do anything else, so the flavor was always the same. One of the most trustworthy foods Sakuta knew.

“Fair, I have never been betrayed by any mackerels. Maybe I can trust you.”

Minagi gave that some thought. After a solid ten seconds, she finally released his hands.

“I’m glad you agree. I’ll be going now.”

Best not to wear out his welcome. If anyone saw this, he’d be demonized. Who would ever believe Minagi had forced him into the stall with her? Everyone would assume he’d been the one who dragged her into the men’s room against her will.

He tried to turn and leave, but Minagi’s hand grabbed the latch first.

“……I thought we had an agreement.”

“I need proof I can trust you.”

Easier said than done.

“I swear on a dried mackerel.”

“I need something more concrete.”

“Should I sign a statement?”

“Hold on. I’m thinking…”

Minagi held a palm up in his face. The universal “stop” pose.

“How long should I hold on?”

Five seconds? Five minutes? Five hours? Different people worked on different scales of time.

Sakuta did not want to be in this position for another second. He wanted out, now. Being in a men’s bathroom stall with a girl was far too risky.

But Minagi did not appear to have heard his question at all. She was making noises with her nose, eyes on the ceiling, racking her mind.

This girl was in a world of her own.

After a solid thirty seconds, she said, “Got it,” and looked back at Sakuta.

He didn’t get anything. Still, he was pretty sure if he waited, she’d explain.

So he waited, but the next thing that popped out of Minagi’s mouth was mind-boggling.

“You can touch my boobs,” she declared.

“……”

For lack of better options, he blinked several times like he wanted to make sure that time had not actually stopped.

“Huh?” he said at long last.

Had he misheard her? He must have. If not, then there must be some other meaning of boobs that he wasn’t familiar with. Perhaps high school girls these days were all into some other sort of “boob”-based trend. He’d have to ask Tomoe later. She’d probably just turn beet red and go, “Senpai, you can’t just ask people that!”

“I said you can touch my boobs.”

“……”

“These boobs.”

“Yeah, that word’s come up enough times for one conversation.”

Sadly, he had not misheard anything. Nor was there any hidden meaning. These were the boobs Sakuta knew and loved.

“Are you more of an ass man, Azusagawa?” she asked, crooking her head.

“If I had to pick, sure.”

“Then go ahead.”

Minagi turned around and stuck her butt up in his direction.

“Is this some sort of custom or ritual I don’t know about?”

“Think of it like hush money.”

“……”

He’d suspected as much but had been hoping otherwise. What circuits had gotten crossed inside her mind? There was clearly a short somewhere.

“Afraid I’m not into buns of steel. I’m more of a peach-butt man.”

Brushing her off, he lowered the lid of the toilet, then took a seat, making an old-man noise as he sat down. It seemed like this discussion was going to take a while, so he’d rather handle it sitting down.

Also, he was still tired from all that running.

“So you wanna go all the way.”

“I did not say that.”

“You don’t want to?”

“……”

“You got real quiet,” Minagi said with a wicked grin. “But I’ve heard the first time hurts. And I’d rather not catch any weird diseases.”

“I do not have cooties.”

“Sure. Well, if you insist, I guess we could…”

Seemingly convinced, she unzipped her jacket. Sakuta wasn’t sure where she was going with this, but she took the jacket off and then started to peel off the gym shirt under it. He got an eyeful of her tight waist and belly button.

“Will you listen?” he said, grabbing the hem of her shirt and pulling it back down. “I never said I wanted to.”

“But you thought it.”

“If I’m gonna get hot and heavy, it’ll be with Mai.”

“I’ll admit I can’t exactly compete with Sakurajima. But I do have a rockin’ bod.”

What he’d seen of her midriff had made that much clear. She’d had the kind of curves anyone would want to throw their arms around. Her beautiful tan was also very tantalizing.

“……Do you not have a boyfriend, Ootsu?”

“Why?”

“I’d feel sorry for him.”

“I don’t, so we’re good. People ask me out a lot, but they always break up with me inside of a month.”

“Because you’re always at volleyball practice and never have time for dates?”

“How’d you know?”

Sakuta knew what it was like to have a busy girlfriend, even if it was in a different line of work. Not that he’d ever consider breaking up with Mai.

“So you don’t have a boyfriend… Anyone you’re sweet on? No one?”

“Well…no.”

She denied it but sounded curiously uncertain. She probably had someone in mind, but…perhaps not a crush she could easily admit to. It was the first time the wind in her sails had flagged; she was being downright evasive.

Had she fallen for a dude with a girlfriend?

Maybe she was friends with the girl.

Sakuta could only hope he wasn’t married.

“Enough about me! Back to the hush money.”

Minagi snapped out of it quick, leaning in.

“I really don’t need or want any.”

He put his hands on her shoulders, gently pushing her away.

“My brother said dudes love to sample.”

Perhaps this brother of hers was why she seemed so comfortable around boys.

“I don’t need any weird diseases, either.”

“Well, I don’t have any!”

“Really?”

“See for yourself !”

Minagi put her hands on the door, thrusting her butt at him.

How was she this uninhibited?

Did playing beach volleyball in those racy outfits just blow those hang-ups away? Maybe it did, maybe it didn’t.

“You’re thinking something rude about beach volleyball right now, aren’t you?” she asked when he said nothing. She had read him like a book. “Just to be clear, competing in bikinis is a bit awkward.”

Her tone said otherwise. But he didn’t think she was lying; it was awkward, but she’d long since accepted it. And what she said next proved as much.

“But the fact that beach volleyball is known for that stuff just shows we’re not good enough yet. We’ve gotta win and win and be the best in the world so that everyone starts enjoying the actual matches instead.”

“Cool, good luck with that.”

“Wow, you did not mean that.”

Sakuta had only just met her—it was hard to care. He was simply saying what he thought she wanted to hear because she had him locked in a toilet stall, and he felt like that alone was praiseworthy.

But if they’d gotten sidetracked, great. Might as well keep the topic on other things.

“Since when does our school have a beach volleyball team?”

“It doesn’t,” Minagi said, winking. “I’m on the Hiratsuka club team.”

“They have those?”

He had seen beach volleyball nets set up on the coast nearby. There’d been some at Kugenuma when he’d gone to see the fireworks with Rio and Yuuma last summer.

Maybe coastal regions were just compatible with the sport.

“Is that a team sport?”

“Pairs. Two on two. Getting curious?”

“About your partner. Is she a Minegahara student?”

If she was, Tomoe would have mentioned her when she was talking Minagi up.

“Nope, the school one station down.”

“Aha.”

She didn’t need to name the school. The station next to Shichirigahama was called Kamakura High School Station.

“Her name’s Kaho Hamamatsu. She’s great at serving and receiving. Flawless tosses. Always puts the ball right where I want it to be.”

She must be picturing her partner’s face. Minagi was looking at Sakuta, but her eyes were focused on something else.

“And the food she cooks when we’re traveling for away games is all amazing.”

Minagi clearly had a lot of faith in Kaho. The expression on her face was happy, relaxed.

“Sounds like she’ll make a great wife someday.”

“Huh? Oh, sure…”

Sakuta was just repeating a cliché, but Minagi’s cheer dissipated.

“Yeah,” she said. “Kaho will make someone very happy.”

It felt like only her words were in agreement.

“Welp. Good luck with all them matches and practice,” he said, getting off the toilet lid. “I should really get going.”

“Mm, okay.”

He tried to move past her.

“Wait, we’re not done yet!” she yelped, grabbing him again. “Are you sure you don’t want to?”

“If I lay a finger on you, you’ll have me over a barrel.”

If he cheated and word got out, he’d be doomed.

Sakuta was pretty sure that was why Minagi kept doing her best to seduce him. He didn’t have to actually do anything; if he touched her at all, that’d be enough. The fact that he’d given in to temptation would become leverage. All she’d have to say was “…or I could tell Sakurajima…” and he’d have to do whatever she said. He’d be silenced for good.

“Tch, was it that obvious?”

He’d confronted her about the scheme, but Minagi didn’t seem fazed at all. She had nerves of steel. Maybe those came naturally to people who spent a lot of time in the world of beach volleyball.

But that was why his (mild) interest in her had given way to one looming question.

Why was Minagi hiding in a toilet?

He hadn’t known her long, but the more they talked, the less clear that became.

It was hard to get a read on her. How much did she mean what she said and how much was a joke? There wasn’t much he could say for certain.

Sakuta had come in not caring, but he was starting to wonder why.

But not enough that he planned to outright ask. He was never one to stick his nose in other people’s problems.

“Azusagawa, you’re exactly the man I heard you were.”

Minagi’s voice pulled him out of his reverie.

“Your source being?”

“Kunimi.”

Right, Yuuma had mentioned she was in his class.

“What sort of terrible things has he been saying about me?”

“He said you only value what’s actually valuable.”

“Doesn’t everyone…?”

“Still…if Kunimi trusts you, I guess I can.”

Minagi was nodding to herself.

Sakuta was really beginning to wonder what the point was of this whole exchange.

“Can I get back this time trapped in a toilet?”

He had not expected Yuuma—who wasn’t even here—to somehow resolve this predicament. Yuuma hadn’t even said a word or lifted a single finger.

Everyone knew him and trusted him.

“I really am going this time.”

“If you tell anyone, I’ll swear you groped me in the men’s room.”

“Fine, but if you do, I will grope the hell out of your ass.”

It just wouldn’t be worth it otherwise.

And his joke did get a big burst of laughter from her.

Sakuta stumbled wearily out of the men’s room and headed for the science lab in search of solace.

It had water, alcohol lamps, beakers, and instant coffee.

He was in desperate need of some real rest. The back-and-forth with Minagi had taken more out of him than the Moving Ball Toss. He was bone-tired.

He knocked first before opening the lab door, but their school was in the middle of the sports festival. There were next to no odds that anyone but Rio was here.

Without waiting for a reply, he flung the door open and found Rio with her back to him. She was standing at the window and talking to Yuuma outside.

When they saw him come in, both turned his way, like he’d nailed the timing.

“Good! I thought you’d vanished on us,” Yuuma said.

He moved across the room to join them at the window.

“Is there another no-show?”

“We still haven’t found Ootsu,” Yuuma admitted.

Minagi was in the second-floor men’s room.

Sakuta almost blurted that out but choked the words back down. If he blew her cover, he’d be forced to grope her ass. Thoroughly.

“The Ball Toss is over. What’s the problem?”

“She was in other events, too,” Rio said, clearly unconcerned. But she did give him a look of pity.

“How many others?” Sakuta asked, his heart sinking.

“The Scavenger Race, the Ball Roll, the Three-Legged Race, and the Relay Race at the end.”

Now Sakuta wanted to hide in the men’s room, too.

5

Long thin clouds swam across the clear fall skies like sardines.

A massive catch.

There was a gentle breeze blowing with a classic autumnal chill.

And beneath that sky, on the grounds of Minegahara High, the crowds were going wild for the third round of the Scavenger Race. Mostly boys from the baseball, soccer, and basketball teams—it was essentially a cross-team competition.

Six players were in each round, two from each color team. Once they’d drawn slips of paper, the hunt was on. None of them had been able to locate the items they were supposed to find yet, eliciting cheers and jeers from the audience.

It was a fun event, appropriate for a festival, and Sakuta was watching from the center of the grounds—at the back of the group waiting for the next round.

A buzz-cut baseball boy with a yellow headband was first across the finish line. Dragging the school nurse after him. Had his piece of paper specified the school nurse, or had it just been “adult woman”?

“The yellow team has now slipped past the red team and are in the lead! Blue team, hang in there!”

The broadcast club’s announcement got the yellow team supporters on their feet. Blearily watching them, Sakuta muttered, “Why am I here?”

“Someone who was signed up for the Scavenger Race was absent, and you’re our official alternate,” Rio reminded him. She was in line, right in front of him. Looking every bit as depressed as he was. She had to take part in the fourth round. Sakuta would be in the fifth and final round of the Scavenger Race. Whether he wanted to be or not.

“Azusagawa, you do know the rules?”

“When the starting pistol goes off, there’s a fifty-meter dash to the box where we draw lots. Then we’ve gotta find whatever’s written on our piece of paper, do a half lap of the track, and cross the finish line.”

Quite a lot of running on top of the scavenger part.

By this point, the last member of the third round made it in.

“Time for round four!”

Rio got up.

“Knock ’em dead,” he said.

She just sighed and moved to the start line.

All six participants were soon in place. All girls. The one to beat was likely that towering basketball-team girl. But basically all of them looked faster than a nerd like Rio. Rio seemed acutely conscious of that fact, and her head was drooping.

There was a bang, and they all ran off.

First, the fifty-meter dash. One player after another shoved their hands in the box. Rio was the sixth to draw—already in last place.

She unfolded the slip of paper and then, for some reason, turned around and came running back to the starting location. Right to where Sakuta was on standby.

Before he could ask why, she grabbed his arm.

“Come.”

“Huh?”

“Just come.”

It seemed he’d been scavenged. Rio yanked, so he started running the required half lap of the track. Rio had been the first to locate her quarry, so she was in first place. But the basketball girl was coming up behind them with the principal in tow.

She would definitely pass them.

“They’re catching up fast,” Sakuta said.

“So? Second place is good enough,” Rio scoffed.

Then a voice called from the stands.

“Futaba! Run!”

It was Yuuma. The blue team was seated by the bend of the track, and he’d been at the front of the crowd.

“Sakuta, don’t slack off !”

These rude words were soon left in the dust.

“Azusagawa, um…,” Rio began, out of breath. No more words came.

“I gotcha. Let’s give it a shot.”

Sakuta took Rio’s hand and sped up—as fast as he could without tripping them. Sakuta was hardly good at running, but he was still faster than Rio.

“Wait! Too fast……,” she grumbled, desperately trying to keep up.

“Five more meters!”

He glanced back, and the basketball girl and principal were right on their heels.

If the track had been five meters longer, they would’ve lost. But since it wasn’t, Sakuta and Rio crossed the finish line first.

“Blue team takes first!”

Now they just had to prove they’d done the scavenger part right.

“Futaba…what…were you supposed to find?” he gasped, badly out of breath.

“……This,” Rio said, shoulders heaving. She handed the paper over to the judge, too tired to make excuses.

It said Friend.

“What was the plan if someone with no friends drew it?” Sakuta felt like the staff in charge should think these things through. “You could have just grabbed Kunimi,” he added.

“You were…clearly…closer…”

Rio was always practical like that. But Sakuta was pretty sure she’d have come to him even if Yuuma had been closer.

“I hate that it worked,” Rio said, laughing.

That came out of nowhere, yet Sakuta knew what she meant. She was laughing at herself for trying harder just because Yuuma told her to. That wasn’t lingering affection—although she did have that in spades. But this was an emotion that couldn’t be categorized that easily and was probably best laughed off.

“Good luck with yours, Azusagawa,” Rio said, catching her breath.

He felt like he’d already done more than enough, but he had his own race to run next. He turned to the start line and found everyone else already in place.

The girl at the end of the row was yelling at him.

“Hurry up, Azusagawa!”

She was waving him over, scowling—Saki Kamisato, wearing an admin committee armband.

Being any later would attract unwanted attention, so without waiting to catch his breath, he hustled over.

“Too slow!”

He’d come pretty quick but still earned himself a glare. Then again, she’d never once smiled at him, so this was just her default behavior.

“Complain to whoever wrote the ‘Friend’ one.”

“That was me.”

“……”

The world was a much smaller place than Sakuta had ever imagined. He was still reeling from that realization when the fifth race started.

Unlike the fourth race, this one was all boys. Sakuta had been forced to join the previous round, so he lagged behind and was last to draw.

“Let the leftover be a good one,” he prayed, opening it up.

The slip of paper said Something sparkly.

“Way too vague.”

Maybe it was meant to be funny, but he would’ve preferred a specific target.

Annoyed, he scanned the stands.

Then his eyes landed on someone that made him go, “Oh. She’s sparkly.”

He made a beeline for the general audience seats, crossing the rope and yelling, “Toyohama, come with me!”

“Hmm? Me?”

“You’re my only hope!”

Rattled, Nodoka took his hand, and he pulled her onto the track.

“What for?!” she wailed, but she ran with him toward the goal. Her golden hair glittered with every step. No one would argue with this selection.

Sakuta finished his half lap with confidence and was first across the finish line.

And the scavenger race judge approved his choice.

Nothing sparkles like an idol.

“My whole body’s gonna ache tomorrow…,” Sakuta muttered as he stood in a corner of the grounds. The Obstacle Race was underway, but he was too worn out to get off the concrete step he’d found.

“It wasn’t that long a run, Sakuta. You’re really out of shape.”

This brutal takedown came from Nodoka, who was standing next to him. She’d run as fast as he had yet seemed unfazed.

“Unlike you, I haven’t gone through any grueling training.”

“I never did anything like that.”

“Then explain how you can sing and dance for ten songs straight.”

Nodoka was a member of Sweet Bullet, an idol unit with choreography even an amateur could tell was pretty intense. They all wound up soaked in sweat. And yet they carried on dancing with huge smiles on their faces—which was clearly proof they’d endured Spartan training exercises.

How had Nodoka packed that much energy into her slender frame?

“Your eyes are so dead right now.”

“This is a gaze of respect,” Sakuta said, too tired to even lift his head.

“How are you this tired already? Get some exercise.”

Nodoka shook her head, appalled.

“I exercised today.”

Earlier, he’d been in the Moving Ball Toss, and now he’d been forced to run the Scavenger Race twice.

“I mean every day.”

Sakuta had known that, obviously. That was why he’d played dumb. He had little interest in wearing himself out regularly.

“The beach is close by. Go jogging.”

“What do beaches have to do with jogging?”

“Doesn’t it sound fun? Running along the coast?”

“I run myself sick every year.”

“Hmm?”

“Our school does a marathon at the start of spring. On the beach below the school.”

Probably instituted by someone who thought like Nodoka. There’s a beach right here; why not take a run on it?

And fair, at the beginning of the race, the sea breeze and the sound of the surf were nice. But the fun lasted about a minute, tops. The Minegahara Marathon on Shichirigahama Beach quickly turned into hell on earth.

Running on sand was way worse than asphalt. It offered little resistance and killed your legs in minutes, leaving them an aching mess. It was less a marathon than…a grueling training exercise. By the time the runners reached the finish line, their knees were chattering, and just getting home was a real feat.

And then the muscle pains hit the day after. Insanely bad ones. It took a full week to recover. And that meant hell at work, which made him resent it all the more.

“Nice. Wish I could join you.”

“The beach belongs to everyone. You can go now!”

“Not feeling it. Also, Sakuta.”

“Mm?”

He looked up and found Nodoka scanning her surroundings.

“We’re getting a lot of looks.”

“Everyone’s going, ‘That girl’s super hot. Which school is she from?’ ”

“Are you making fun of me?” she snarled, glaring at him.

“That was a compliment.”

Students from other schools attending culture or sports festivals all looked at least 50 percent cooler or cuter, but even accounting for that, Nodoka was clearly on the good-looking side.

Her self-evaluations were a little low because she was comparing herself with the exceptional.

“My sister goes here.”

“Yes, my Mai is a student here.”

“She’s not yours! She’s mine!”

“You have got to learn to let go.”

Nodoka’s problem was that she was constantly comparing herself with Mai. Trading bodies had helped clear some of her baggage up, but years of inferiority were not so easily resolved. Sakuta knew she’d have to slowly work on it over time.

“Point is, my sister goes here, so they’re not looking at me.”

“Could be they just haven’t seen blond hair. We are in Japan.”

“Plenty of girls dye theirs.”

Maybe not as bright a blond as Nodoka’s, but there were plenty of boys and girls with lighter hair colors.

So these looks were probably for several reasons. A cute girl from another school…was certainly part of it. So were the blond locks. A gaudy hairstyle, striking makeup—yet she was wearing the uniform of a famous Yokohama all-girls school. That was a surprising enough combination to attract attention.

Of course, it was also notable that she was with Sakuta. Everyone in school knew the stories about the hospitalization incident, and lately his relationship with Mai had become public knowledge. She’d just given a whole press conference addressing that.

People would naturally wonder what Nodoka was doing with him. What exactly was their relationship?

What should he say if someone asked?

Should he just say she was an idol who might become a pseudo sister-in-law one day? That would probably just confuse people…

“Right, Toyohama.”

“Mm?” she said absently. Her attention was on the antics of the Obstacle Race, which were drawing big laughs from the crowd.

“Why are you here?”

“Huh? Now?” She blinked, then gave him a baffled look.

“Shouldn’t you be out there doing idol things?”

“We just had a solo concert, so we’ve got a break from lessons this week. When I told my sister, she said she had a ticket to the sports festival…so I figured I might as well come see what you were up to.”

“I’d rather Mai came.”

If she was cheering for him, maybe he could have tried a bit harder.

“She’s here.”

“……Wait, really?”

First he’d heard of it. She’d said last night she wouldn’t be taking part.

“Where?”

He got to his feet, looking around. A quick scan failed to locate her. He was sure he could pick her out of any crowd.

“She made lunch, so she said to meet her in the empty classroom on the third floor.”

“Tell me that first!”

“You dragged me into the Scavenger Race before I could.”

If Mai was here, he wasn’t about to hang out in the corner like this. The Obstacle Race was the last of the morning’s events; no one would complain if he ditched a little early.

With that in mind, he started toward the school building.

“Oh, wait, Sakuta,” Nodoka said, tugging his sleeve.

“I want Mai to comfort me ASAP.”

“That girl over there.”

Nodoka was looking at the general admission section of the stands.

“The one in the gray tracksuit.”

The girl in question didn’t seem interested in the Obstacle Race. She was looking around, like she was trying to find someone.

She seemed roughly their age. But the tracksuit was the wrong color, which stood out.

“Why, do you know her?”

“Not personally. But she plays beach volleyball.”

“……A lot of that going around.”

Was that the lucky sport of the day?

“You don’t know her, Sakuta?”

“I can guess. She’s a junior athlete like Ootsu?”

This was new information to him, but he brought it up anyway. He didn’t know anything more than that, but it seemed like all he needed to know.

“Exactly, she’s Minagi Ootsu’s partner. What was her name again?”

Nodoka took out her phone and did a search.

“Kaho Hamamatsu,” he said.

He’d heard that name earlier today, from Minagi Ootsu herself.

“Oh, right. See?”

Nodoka showed him her screen. There was a photo on it, from the awards ceremony of some sporting event. Two girls stood on the highest platform, beaming. One of them was clearly Minagi, the girl he’d just met in the men’s room. And the girl with her looked a lot like the girl in the gray tracksuit Nodoka had pointed out.

Kaho was here looking for somebody.

Presumably Minagi.

He could have told her where Minagi was, but if a total stranger rolled up and said, “Ootsu’s in the men’s room,” she’d likely freak out. And if she was here to find her, why not just call her phone? It wasn’t Sakuta’s problem.

“Welp, I’m going to see Mai,” he said, and he headed for the school.

“I’m coming with!” Nodoka yelped, chasing after him.

Sakuta got Nodoka some slippers at the guest entrance, then went around to the regular entrance to change into his own.

He got them out of the locker and put his shoes in. At that point, he heard footsteps approaching from the interior. A light, poised gait he’d recognize anywhere.

Just as he predicted, Mai came around the corner of the lockers.

Her eyes met Sakuta’s.

“You’re late,” she said, cross.

“Were you counting every second you were away from me?”

“You threw such a fit when I said I couldn’t be in the sports festival.”

He’d been a snot, so she pinched his cheek.

“Ow. Ow!”

“You’re smiling.”

“I’m just happy you’re here to fuss over me.”

“Is that what this is?”

As they bantered, he heard slippers approaching. Nodoka caught up.

“Oh, Mai, you changed,” she said, the second she caught sight of her sister.

“Being in uniform would stand out today.”

Mai’s hand let go of Sakuta’s cheek. She was wearing the school tracksuit. Her hair was in two loose braids, and she had fake glasses on. It gave her an adorable baseball-team-manager vibe, which was novel.

“My Mai is even cute in a tracksuit.”

“You’ve seen it before.”

“Not very often.”

Mai probably changed into it for gym class, but they were in different years, and he didn’t have many chances to see her wearing this around school.

“If I’d known you’d make tracksuits this cute, I’d have made more of an effort.”

He was looking Mai all over, burning her into his retinas.

“Don’t ogle my sister!”

Nodoka’s foot shot out and tried to stomp on his foot. He hastily dodged.

“Don’t dodge!”

“Don’t try to step on me.”

If Mai stepped on him, it was a reward, but if Nodoka did that, it was no fun at all.

“Other students will be coming in once lunch starts, so I’m going on ahead.”

Mai left, leaving Sakuta and Nodoka to their squabbles. Sakuta hurried after her. They climbed the stairs together. Nodoka caught up on the other side of Mai and wrapped her arm around Mai’s. She shot Sakuta a look like “Aren’t you jealous?”

“So, Mai…”

“You’re filthy, Sakuta. Don’t get clingy.”

“Then what should I do?”

Minagi probably knew better. She just couldn’t bring herself to take that step. That was all this was about.

“Get out of that box.”

“And?”

“Go see Hamamatsu.”

Sakuta didn’t mince words, and Minagi didn’t seem the least bit surprised. He knew she’d known all along. Once she saw Kaho, she’d get a response. And that was what scared her.

She didn’t want to make it weird.

She didn’t want to make things awkward.

But most of all, she was scared she’d ruin a relationship she loved.

“But…,” Minagi began.

Her voice was so feeble and it sounded like she was about to launch into an excuse, so Sakuta spoke firmly.

“You can’t just go back to the way you were. Give it up.”

Once they knew love was in the air, neither could pretend otherwise. It was impossible to act like nothing happened. Knowing made them conscious of it. They’d be actively trying to pretend everything was normal.

Maybe after a few years, this would be something they could laugh about, but neither Sakuta nor Minagi was old enough for that now.

“……”

Minagi’s lips were zipped again. The silence proved she understood and was processing what he’d said. She’d gone quiet so she could sort out her feelings.

But thirty seconds came and went, and she still said nothing. Thirty seconds became a minute.

Then the silence was broken by someone else entirely.

“Um…”

A hesitant voice.

Sakuta turned around to find Kaho Hamamatsu not five yards away.

“Sorry for earlier. I kinda turned tail and ran.”

“Don’t worry about it.”

“I shouldn’t have done that to Mai Sakurajima.”

“I’m pretty sure she didn’t mind.”

Mai had been mega-famous since she was a child star; there wasn’t much that could catch her by surprise anymore.

“Something you need?” Sakuta asked.

Inside the vaulting box, he heard Minagi gulp.

Kaho herself seemed super tense. She had her fingers tied up in knots, restlessly moving them around. Her legs were trembling. But her eyes were locked right on Sakuta.

“Do you know where Minagi is?” she asked.

“You mean Minagi Ootsu?”

“Yes. I’m her beach volleyball partner.”

“Kaho Hamamatsu, right? I know that much.”

“Thanks.” She bobbed her head awkwardly. It was obvious she wasn’t used to strangers knowing her name. “You were talking about Minagi earlier, right?”

She was clearly referring to his conversation with Mai at the vending machine.

“We were. But that doesn’t mean I know where she is.”

“Oh…”

She looked crestfallen. Dejected. So clearly disappointed it made Sakuta feel guilty for lying to her. A proper pang of conscience.

“Have you called her?”

“I have. Texts, emails, calls…no answers.”

Come to think of it, when he’d collected Minagi’s clothes, there’d been no phone in the pile. Maybe she’d left it with her things in her classroom.

“Sorry I can’t be more help.”

“No…thanks anyway.”

He’d been useless, but Kaho bowed her head anyway. That made him feel even worse. He knew exactly where Minagi was.

“If I see Ootsu, I’ll tell her you’re looking for her.”

She was right here in the vaulting box, so he essentially already had.

“Thanks a lot. Oh, but…”

“But?”

“……”

He could hazard a guess why she was hesitating.

Minagi was clearly avoiding her.

She must have worked that out…and it was making her nervous. Nevertheless, she said, “Please do.”

Kaho’s head came up. There was a sad look in her eyes that she tried to hide behind a forced smile.

“Okay. Will do,” Sakuta promised.

She seemed slightly taken aback by his serious reply, but she bobbed her head one more time and darted off toward the field.

As he watched her go, Sakuta said, “Yo, Ootsu.”

Minagi didn’t answer, but he kept talking anyway.

“Hamamatsu’s legs were quivering. She’s just as scared as you are. But she found the courage to come and talk to you. You gonna leave it all up to her?”

Minagi said nothing.

“Ootsu?”

He tapped the vaulting box but got nothing. No sounds at all.

“You’re kidding…”

Knowing what he was likely in for, Sakuta said a prayer and lifted the top layer.

“……”

As he’d feared, Minagi was no longer inside. The tracksuit he’d loaned her had been left behind.

“And I made that nice little speech, too.”

How long had he been talking to himself ? Wondering would only make him feel worse. He went ahead and put his tracksuit back on.

Where had she teleported to this time? There wasn’t a discernible pattern, as far as Sakuta could tell, so his only option was to walk all over the place again. Weirdly, he was fairly confident Minagi was still on school grounds. The first two jumps had been, and even if she was running from Kaho, Minagi clearly felt like she had to resolve this mess today. She had basically said as much herself.

He should probably start by finding Mai and Rio and sharing what he knew. But as that thought crossed his mind…

“Azusagawa, why are you over here? I said the tent on the field!”

He heard Saki yelling at him. She was marching his way, looking like a demon. And Yuuma and Tomoe were scrambling after her.

“Sakuta, there you are! The Ball Roll!”

“Move it, Senpai! It’s about to start!”

They were both waving furiously.

He had some choice words he would’ve liked to say about all this but he didn’t want to get chewed out any more than he already had. He hustled toward the field, pushing the cart ahead of him.

“Run, Sakuta, run!”

“I am!”

“Ugh, I’m bushed…”

Sakuta had played his part in the Ball Roll, but the event wasn’t over. For the moment, he was crouching to the side of the track.

“I can’t…move…a muscle…,” Tomoe gasped, sitting next to him. Her shoulders heaved with every breath. But there was a smile on her face.

Tomoe was quite pleased with their results.

They’d received the giant ball while in second place and worked together to get around the obstacles on their half of the course. They hadn’t managed to overtake the yellow team, but they were fast enough that the red team couldn’t catch up with them.

Sakuta and Tomoe’s turn had ended safely without them doing anything noteworthy—good or bad. That was exactly the way Tomoe liked it. She was relieved.

Nodoka was waving to him from the school building. She must need him for something.

“Gonna hit the can,” he told Tomoe.

Then he headed in Nodoka’s direction. When he got there, she snapped, “You could’ve run.”

“So?” he asked.

He hadn’t lied to Tomoe after all.

“What?!” Nodoka clearly didn’t get it, but he left her there, heading back to school alone.

Inside the entrance, Sakuta hastily made for the second floor. Every step on the staircase hurt his tired legs.

A quick scan of the long second-story hallway revealed no one was around. Rio had originally been posted on bathroom watch duty, but she was no longer here; it had been over an hour, so she must not have stuck around. Mai had probably let her know when she’d found Minagi.

Sakuta slipped into the deserted men’s room, scrambled over the stall in the back, and retrieved Minagi’s pile of clothes. This was hard work for his exhausted body, but he brought everything with him to the third floor.

Two people were waiting outside the girls’ changing room. Mai and Rio.

Mai had been in touch with Rio.

Sakuta’s attention was all on Mai, though. She was dressed different. Shorts and a short-sleeved gym shirt. Mai’s figure was far too impressive, and those shorts revealed her beautiful legs up to the top of her knees. A shame he couldn’t see the thighs as well, but any glimpse of her bare legs was a gift.

“Gimme those,” Mai said, snatching Minagi’s clothes from him. She knocked on the changing room door, said, “Coming in,” and vanished inside.

A minute later, she came out alone.

She was back in her tracksuit. Bare-leg time had ended as soon as it began.

Her eyes met Sakuta’s, and she beckoned to him.

“You need help changing?” he joked, closing in. The crack doubled in size.

“Sakurajima’s tracksuit smelled really good!”

Of all the things to say. She’d mentioned being unsure if she was into girls, but he thought this basically settled that question.

“Mai’s mine. You can’t have her.”

“So you are actually dating.”

“About Kaho…,” she murmured, still wavering. “She came here for me. I’ve gotta meet her halfway.”

“So?”

“But every time I try…I wind up somewhere else.”

“Gotcha. Gimme a sec.”

Sakuta turned toward Rio.

“So, Futaba.”

“What?”

“Let me first ask this,” Rio said, eyes over his shoulder—on Minagi, peering through the crack in the door.

“What?”

“Azusagawa, have you seen her vanish?”

The first time she’d vanished from inside a stall in the men’s room.

Same for the second.

The third time she’d been inside the vaulting box.

Three teleports, and he hadn’t seen any of them happen.

“……No, I haven’t.”

He’d simply found the empty tracksuit afterward.

“Then that might be a condition.”

Sakuta had no idea what she was driving at.

“Meaning?” he asked.

Rio’s answer came in her usual flat voice.

“Preventing teleportation might be surprisingly simple.”

Approximately twenty minutes later, Sakuta was standing in the middle of the school grounds. He was in line for the Three-Legged Race.

Minagi was next to him. Their ankles were tied together with a headband.

“Why is this happening?”

Sakuta knew the reason. This was Rio’s “surprisingly simple” solution. The logic went something like this…

“I believe she’ll be unable to teleport if someone keeps their eyes on her. As long as she’s under observation, she’ll stay at her fixed location.”

“Then should we just watch her constantly? Without blinking?”

“Azusagawa, do you know what day it is?”

“Sunday. The sports festival day.”

“So if you and me and Sakurajima get her to the school grounds without losing sight of her, then the entire student body will keep her in place.”

“But what if all three of us accidentally blink at once?”

“Then she might teleport.”

“We just have to avoid blinking until we’re outside. I always go a minute or two without blinking during shoots; that’s no big deal.”

Thanks to the famous actress Mai Sakurajima’s unexpected talent, they’d successfully escorted Minagi outside.

It would have been nice to immediately start her showdown with Kaho, but the blue team found Minagi first.

When people asked where she’d been, Sakuta just said, “She was worn out from beach volleyball practice and fell asleep.”

That earned her some concern, but Minagi hurriedly explained, “I ate lunch and felt way better!” with a big smile.

She had been signed up for the Three-Legged Race, so she had to participate. And Sakuta got roped into it, too because someone else had gotten injured… This was just not his day.

Rio suggested that joining an event would increase the eyes on Minagi, but he really didn’t think it was necessary for him to be paired with her.

“Ugh…”

How could he not sigh?

“Your happiness is getting away,” Minagi said as she finished tying the knot.

“Don’t worry. Mai will just bring it back.”

“Nice. Keep her close!”

Minagi cackled, but her face were still pretty tense. She wasn’t worrying about the Three-Legged Race. She kept her head down and eyes on the ground because she knew someone must be looking at her.

“Is Kaho watching?”

“Not sure.”

Sakuta did a quick scan of the crowd but failed to locate Kaho. The school had a thousand students to begin with, and loads of family and friends were visiting as well. There were too many people in too many places.

The only face he picked out immediately was Nodoka’s. Mai was next to her. She was doing her braids-and-glasses combo, so no one around had recognized her. Nodoka was attracting all the attention like a lightning rod.

Mai saw Sakuta looking and flashed him a quick smile.

“Ootsu, which would you prefer?”

“Huh?”

“Do you want her watching or not?”

“I want her watching.”

Minagi didn’t hesitate. She might not have raised her head yet, but there was an intensity behind her words—and a soft note on top, reserved for Kaho.

“Then she’s watching.”

“What if I said I didn’t want her watching?”

“She’d also be watching.”

That was how these things worked.

Before they could say anything else, the starting pistol went off.

Two pairs from each color—so six pairs in all—set off around the track. A half lap—the next pair was waiting for the baton around the bend.

“The Three-Legged Race is a relay race?”

“Apparently.”

Worryingly, Minagi was in the same boat he was. She really had slept through the event-selection homeroom.

“Well, we’re at the end of the line, so let’s assume we’re the anchors. We just gotta get the baton and hit the finish line.”

Minagi was shrugging this off, but the Three-Legged Race was near the end of the sports festival—the crowd was way more worked up than Sakuta had expected. This was not an event that depended solely on running skills, so it was hard to predict who’d win—that helped keep it exciting.

The second pair was handing the baton to the third.

That left only the fourth—the anchors. Sakuta and Minagi.

Minagi put her arm round Sakuta’s waist. The sudden grab made him grunt.

“Grab my shoulders,” she said, so he put an arm around hers. Two tight grips, very stable. He could really tell how strong her core was.

“Start with the tied leg, moving one, two, one, two.”

No time to argue. The baton was approaching fast.

“Got it.”

Minagi kept going “One, two, one two” as they moved into the baton pass zone.

The pair coming toward them was Saki and a first-year boy…who was rather red in the face. He must’ve been incredibly embarrassed. They were in fourth place. The pairs behind them had fumbled the baton pass on the second or third round, so they were a solid half lap behind.

“Here!” Saki grumpily handed the baton over, and they caught it.

“And one, two.” They set off. Minagi kept that rhythm going. “One, two, one, two.”

Their pace was much faster than Sakuta had expected. He nearly stumbled. But if he complained or tried to change speeds, they’d immediately tumble to the ground—all he could do was force his feet to stay on beat.

Ahead of them were two red pairs and a yellow one. Halfway around the bend, they passed the third-place yellow pair. They caught up with the second-place pair at the end of the bend and blew by.

Only the first-place pair left.

But even at a low estimate, they had a solid ten-yard lead.

The finish line was right there. Their half lap was almost over. No way to catch up—

Or so he thought, but the lead team crossed the finish line and kept on going, not slowing down at all. As he wondered why, the broadcast-club commentary answered for him.

“The anchor teams get a full lap! This battle’s not over yet!”

But his legs were dead. He’d gone all out on the assumption they only had to run a half lap.

“You got this, Sakuta!” Yuuma yelled from the blue seats. Unnecessary.

“Senpai, move those feet!”

Was that Tomoe?

She didn’t need to tell him. He was moving his feet. Moving them like his life depended on it. That was the only way he could keep up with Minagi.

The crowd was really going wild now. Cheers were coming from all directions, trying to overwhelm him.

They were through the back straight and on the curve again. Then—

“Minagi! Gooooo!” someone yelled.

He felt Minagi jump. She kept chanting “One, two, one, two,” but her eyes were on the stands at the curve.

On a girl in a gray tracksuit. Kaho Hamamatsu.

Minagi didn’t say a word.

But her arm tightened around his waist.

He had an idea what she wanted. He knew, but he argued, “My legs are dead.”

Despite that, Minagi just snorted. Derisively. Her lips curled gleefully, and she upped the pace of her “One, two, one, two.”

And when Sakuta started to drag behind, her firm grip on his waist pulled him right along.

Three yards to the lead pair. Ten to the goalposts.

At this point, his mind went blank. He couldn’t breathe. His legs felt like lead. The grip on his waist allowed no escape; he was joined to Minagi at the hip.

All he could think about was not falling, and that kept both legs pumping.

They were almost at the finish line.

They were neck and neck with the other pair now. He could almost feel their looks of surprise on his skin. And then they took their last steps.

The finish tape hit Sakuta’s and Minagi’s hips, and they soared across the line, running for a solid twenty yards past it.

They gradually slowed down until finally coming to a halt straight off the track—they hadn’t taken the curve.

The moment they stopped, Sakuta collapsed. He’d never been more out of breath. He’d have liked to grumble but was in no state to speak. His body demanded oxygen.

Meanwhile, Minagi only needed a couple of deep breaths. She had her hands on her hips, standing straight and tall. Here was a true athlete. Kinda cool. Downright badass, even.

Ever since she’d stopped, Minagi’s eyes had been on one thing. On the far corner, where Kaho had been.

The crowds were still buzzing from Sakuta and Minagi’s come-from-behind victory; students were on their feet and jumping around. Sakuta couldn’t find Kaho in the chaos.

But Minagi must have—her eyes were locked on a single point and not budging. Sakuta followed her gaze, and after a minute, Kaho emerged from the Minegahara crowd. She ran toward them, but pulled up short a good ten yards out.

Kaho seemed nervous.

Sakuta wordlessly untied the knot on their feet.

“Kaho,” Minagi said, running over to her. He thought that would be it, but she stopped halfway, turning back to Sakuta. “Thanks, Azusagawa.”

“You’re welcome.”

“Will you take payment in boobs or butt?”

“Got my fill of both during this race,” he said, getting up. “Go on, get,” he said, waving her toward Kaho. The rest was their problem.

“Thanks,” Minagi said again, and then she ran the rest of the way to Kaho, light on her feet.

Sakuta’s feet were deadweights, but he dragged them back toward the school. He was going to rest in class until the sports festival was done and over, no matter what.

Something he remembered in his dreams that slipped away come morning.

That morning, Sakuta Azusagawa was woken by her kiss.

He’d felt her crawl into his bed, and he’d known it must be morning. But his eyes failed to open. She wriggled into the loose sweatshirt he slept in, moved up his stomach to his chest and then out the neck—and finally licked his cheek.

“Five more minutes…,” he muttered, half asleep.

Her answer was another kiss. Well, more of a slurp.

That was impossible to sleep through.

Sakuta gave up and forced his heavy eyelids open.

Before his eyes was the head of a tricolored cat, sticking out of his sweatshirt.

“Meow,” she said, in a rather low voice for a lady cat. Her name was Nasuno.

“Morning, Nasuno.”

“Mew.”

Sakuta turned his eyes toward his alarm clock. It was 6:59 AM…and then it flipped to seven. The alarm started blaring, but he stopped it instantly. The arm that had slipped outside his covers was freezing already.

It was winter. December 24. Christmas Eve.

He was feeling very ready for winter vacation, but sadly, they still had school today. The last day of the second term, which was the day of the end-of-term ceremony.

It would hardly be a big deal if he skipped that. It’d be awfully nice to sleep in, tucked in his warm bed. The ultimate winter luxury.

But not today.

“Better get up.”

Sakuta won the battle quick, despite the chilly room.

“Too cold…”

It was extra nippy this morning.

“I guess they were predicting snow…”

He’d half watched the weather report last night, and there’d been a big cold front moving in. They’d been expecting accumulation in the flat and coastal areas of Kanto. “I’m sure a lot of people will be venturing out for Christmas Eve, but please do watch your step,” the weather lady said.

Last year, Sakuta had no such plans and would have resented the implication, but this year, he was nodding along. I will watch my step, he’d thought. This year, he had plenty of plans.

He pulled Nasuno out of his clothes.

“Mrow,” she said, clearly hungry. He followed her into the living room.

First, he put some kibble in her bowl.

The sound of her crunching away filled the quiet room.

This morning, only Nasuno and Sakuta were home.

Their dad had picked Kaede up just after noon yesterday, and she was spending the night at their grandparents’. They were probably doting on her right that second. It had been a solid two years since they’d seen her…

She wouldn’t be home until the day after tomorrow, the twenty-sixth.

“Stay as long as you like,” he’d told her when she was leaving.

“I’ll be back the twenty-sixth,” Kaede insisted.

She was dead set on that, her glare making it clear he couldn’t change her mind.

He could guess why.

Kaede had things to do when she got back.

Sakuta put a slice of bread in the toaster and fried an egg in the meantime.

Once both were done, he scarfed them down.

He washed the pan and was putting it away when the phone rang.

The number on-screen was his dad’s cell.

He dried his hands, picked up the receiver, and said, “Hello?”

“Oh, Sakuta?” Far too cute a voice to be his dad.

Clearly, this was not his dad but his sister, Kaede.

“What?”

“What do you mean, what?”

He’d just asked, but she got mad at him for it.

“You called me.”

“I didn’t call when I arrived yesterday, so I am now.”

She must have been talking about their grandparents’ house.

“Are Grandma and Grandpa doing okay?”

“They’re good. They wish you came along.”

“I’ll go over eventually. Now go get spoiled enough for both of us.”

“Then I get your Christmas presents and New Year’s money, right?”

How greedy.

“I’ve got Mai, so I can let you have that much.”

Mai had agreed to a date today. They’d be meeting up at six, after she got off work. Given how packed her schedule was, getting to spend Christmas together was a real blessing.

That promise was the only thing that convinced him to get out of bed that morning and go to school instead of sleeping in.

“Mai doesn’t like it when you’re rude.”

It was Christmas. Sakuta would love to do quite a few “rude” things with Mai. As much as he could get away with, no matter what it took to get him there. But telling his sister this would hardly be appropriate, so he held his tongue.

“Actually, Mai thought you’d be here. She suggested we all have cake together.”

“I would be such a third wheel. That’s why I’m here.”

“My Mai would never think that.”

“But you totally would,” Kaede huffed. She didn’t even bother hiding how put out she was.

“Don’t sweat it. Toyohama swears she’s coming right back home after her Christmas concert, so you’d be more of a fourth wheel.”

The third wheel would have dazzling blond hair.

“I’m gonna tell Nodoka you said that.”

“No need, I’ll tell her myself.”

He needed to get that siscon idol to back off a bit.

“……You’re one weird dude,” Kaede muttered.

“I gotta get ready for school. Hanging up.”

“Oh, sorry, wait!”

“Mm? What?”

“Um, er…” Kaede’s voice dwindled away.

“……”

Sakuta said nothing, waiting for her to finish.

“So, uh…”

Even over the phone, he could tell she had something on her mind. It must’ve been really hard for her to say. And that gave Sakuta a good idea what it must be.

“Um, once I get back…”

She’d started big, but her voice dropped to a whisper.

“You need help practicing the walk to school?”

“Why’d you say it for me?!”

He figured she looked as peeved as she sounded. He bet she was pouting so hard her lips stuck out.

“ ’Cause it’s time for me to go.”

He actually had a few minutes to spare, but these types of family discussions made him uncomfortable. Like an itch he couldn’t scratch.

“……Thanks, Sakuta.”

“Hanging up now.”

“Mm, okay.”

She seemed ready to drag this discomfort out, so he wrapped things up.

Nasuno had finished eating and let out a satisfied meow. She began washing her face and scratching the back of her neck with her hind legs.

Looking up from the cat, Sakuta realized Kaede had left her bedroom door open. Her junior high uniform was on a hanger by the closet. She must have gotten it ready before she left yesterday. So the moment she got home, she could put it on and walk to school. So she could go to school every day.

Nasuno meowed again.

It was high time Sakuta got changed and left.

Leaving Nasuno to guard the fort, Sakuta left just before eight.
