As he watched her go, Sakuta said, “Yo, Ootsu.”

Minagi didn’t answer, but he kept talking anyway.

“Hamamatsu’s legs were quivering. She’s just as scared as you are. But she found the courage to come and talk to you. You gonna leave it all up to her?”

Minagi said nothing.

“Ootsu?”

He tapped the vaulting box but got nothing. No sounds at all.

“You’re kidding…”

Knowing what he was likely in for, Sakuta said a prayer and lifted the top layer.

“……”

As he’d feared, Minagi was no longer inside. The tracksuit he’d loaned her had been left behind.

“And I made that nice little speech, too.”

How long had he been talking to himself ? Wondering would only make him feel worse. He went ahead and put his tracksuit back on.

Where had she teleported to this time? There wasn’t a discernible pattern, as far as Sakuta could tell, so his only option was to walk all over the place again. Weirdly, he was fairly confident Minagi was still on school grounds. The first two jumps had been, and even if she was running from Kaho, Minagi clearly felt like she had to resolve this mess today. She had basically said as much herself.

He should probably start by finding Mai and Rio and sharing what he knew. But as that thought crossed his mind…

“Azusagawa, why are you over here? I said the tent on the field!”

He heard Saki yelling at him. She was marching his way, looking like a demon. And Yuuma and Tomoe were scrambling after her.

“Sakuta, there you are! The Ball Roll!”

“Move it, Senpai! It’s about to start!”

They were both waving furiously.

He had some choice words he would’ve liked to say about all this but he didn’t want to get chewed out any more than he already had. He hustled toward the field, pushing the cart ahead of him.

“Run, Sakuta, run!”

“I am!”

12

“Ugh, I’m bushed…”

Sakuta had played his part in the Ball Roll, but the event wasn’t over. For the moment, he was crouching to the side of the track.

“I can’t…move…a muscle…,” Tomoe gasped, sitting next to him. Her shoulders heaved with every breath. But there was a smile on her face.

Tomoe was quite pleased with their results.

They’d received the giant ball while in second place and worked together to get around the obstacles on their half of the course. They hadn’t managed to overtake the yellow team, but they were fast enough that the red team couldn’t catch up with them.

Sakuta and Tomoe’s turn had ended safely without them doing anything noteworthy—good or bad. That was exactly the way Tomoe liked it. She was relieved.

“Oh, Kunimi took the lead!” she shouted.

Sakuta looked up. Yuuma was paired up with a first-year girl, and they’d passed the yellow team right before the finish line, claiming first place. They were already exchanging high fives.

“He is so annoying,” Sakuta grumbled as he rose to his feet. He was still a little out of breath, but he’d caught something glittering out of the corner of his eye.

Nodoka was waving to him from the school building. She must need him for something.

“Gonna hit the can,” he told Tomoe.

Then he headed in Nodoka’s direction. When he got there, she snapped, “You could’ve run.”

“So?” he asked.

“Here,” Nodoka said, handing him her phone. The screen showed an incoming call from Sis. That could only mean Mai.

“What’s up, Mai?”

“I should be asking you. Where have you been?”

She sounded less than pleased.

“I was moving a vaulting box around, then rolling a ball.”

“You’re supposed to be looking for Ootsu.”

“But I did find her. Looking forward to that bath with you.”

“Is she with you now?”

“Nope, she vanished again.”

“Then it doesn’t count. Ootsu’s with me now, so I win.”

“But I found her first!”

“Go get her tracksuit and meet us at the third-floor girls’ changing room.”

“Ah, wait, Mai…!”

He tried to dig in, but she’d already hung up. No interest in his protests.

“What’d she say?” Nodoka asked when he handed the phone back.

“She wants me to hit the can.”

He hadn’t lied to Tomoe after all.

“What?!” Nodoka clearly didn’t get it, but he left her there, heading back to school alone.

Inside the entrance, Sakuta hastily made for the second floor. Every step on the staircase hurt his tired legs.

A quick scan of the long second-story hallway revealed no one was around. Rio had originally been posted on bathroom watch duty, but she was no longer here; it had been over an hour, so she must not have stuck around. Mai had probably let her know when she’d found Minagi.

Sakuta slipped into the deserted men’s room, scrambled over the stall in the back, and retrieved Minagi’s pile of clothes. This was hard work for his exhausted body, but he brought everything with him to the third floor.

Two people were waiting outside the girls’ changing room. Mai and Rio.

Mai had been in touch with Rio.

Sakuta’s attention was all on Mai, though. She was dressed different. Shorts and a short-sleeved gym shirt. Mai’s figure was far too impressive, and those shorts revealed her beautiful legs up to the top of her knees. A shame he couldn’t see the thighs as well, but any glimpse of her bare legs was a gift.

“Gimme those,” Mai said, snatching Minagi’s clothes from him. She knocked on the changing room door, said, “Coming in,” and vanished inside.

A minute later, she came out alone.

She was back in her tracksuit. Bare-leg time had ended as soon as it began.

After another three minutes, the door to the changing room opened again. This time only a crack a few inches wide. Minagi was peering through it.

Her eyes met Sakuta’s, and she beckoned to him.

“You need help changing?” he joked, closing in. The crack doubled in size.

“Sakurajima’s tracksuit smelled really good!”

Of all the things to say. She’d mentioned being unsure if she was into girls, but he thought this basically settled that question.

“Mai’s mine. You can’t have her.”

“So you are actually dating.”

Minagi’s voice went back to normal. It was public knowledge around school, but that didn’t mean it felt real. Probably lot of students felt that way. Dating the Mai Sakurajima just didn’t sound believable. She was someone from TV.

“Is that all?” he asked, and her smile flickered. There was hesitation in her eyes.

“About Kaho…,” she murmured, still wavering. “She came here for me. I’ve gotta meet her halfway.”

“So?”

“But every time I try…I wind up somewhere else.”

Minagi knew she shouldn’t run from this. Her rational mind did, at least. But some part of her was ruled by a fear of how this would turn out. And that emotion was far stronger than she realized. Its roots ran deep. She was so scared Kaho would reject her that she couldn’t stop running—or teleporting.

“Gotcha. Gimme a sec.”

Sakuta turned toward Rio.

“So, Futaba.”

“What?”

“Any way to prevent Ootsu from teleporting?”

“Let me first ask this,” Rio said, eyes over his shoulder—on Minagi, peering through the crack in the door.

“What?”

“Azusagawa, have you seen her vanish?”

The first time she’d vanished from inside a stall in the men’s room.

Same for the second.

The third time she’d been inside the vaulting box.

Three teleports, and he hadn’t seen any of them happen.

“……No, I haven’t.”

He’d simply found the empty tracksuit afterward.

“Then that might be a condition.”

Sakuta had no idea what she was driving at.

“Meaning?” he asked.

Rio’s answer came in her usual flat voice.

“Preventing teleportation might be surprisingly simple.”

Approximately twenty minutes later, Sakuta was standing in the middle of the school grounds. He was in line for the Three-Legged Race.

Minagi was next to him. Their ankles were tied together with a headband.

“Why is this happening?”

Sakuta knew the reason. This was Rio’s “surprisingly simple” solution. The logic went something like this…

“I believe she’ll be unable to teleport if someone keeps their eyes on her. As long as she’s under observation, she’ll stay at her fixed location.”

“Then should we just watch her constantly? Without blinking?”

“Azusagawa, do you know what day it is?”

“Sunday. The sports festival day.”

“So if you and me and Sakurajima get her to the school grounds without losing sight of her, then the entire student body will keep her in place.”

“But what if all three of us accidentally blink at once?”

“Then she might teleport.”

“We just have to avoid blinking until we’re outside. I always go a minute or two without blinking during shoots; that’s no big deal.”

Thanks to the famous actress Mai Sakurajima’s unexpected talent, they’d successfully escorted Minagi outside.

It would have been nice to immediately start her showdown with Kaho, but the blue team found Minagi first.

When people asked where she’d been, Sakuta just said, “She was worn out from beach volleyball practice and fell asleep.”

That earned her some concern, but Minagi hurriedly explained, “I ate lunch and felt way better!” with a big smile.

She had been signed up for the Three-Legged Race, so she had to participate. And Sakuta got roped into it, too because someone else had gotten injured… This was just not his day.

Rio suggested that joining an event would increase the eyes on Minagi, but he really didn’t think it was necessary for him to be paired with her.

“Ugh…”

How could he not sigh?

“Your happiness is getting away,” Minagi said as she finished tying the knot.

“Don’t worry. Mai will just bring it back.”

“Nice. Keep her close!”

Minagi cackled, but her face were still pretty tense. She wasn’t worrying about the Three-Legged Race. She kept her head down and eyes on the ground because she knew someone must be looking at her.

“Is Kaho watching?”

“Not sure.”

Sakuta did a quick scan of the crowd but failed to locate Kaho. The school had a thousand students to begin with, and loads of family and friends were visiting as well. There were too many people in too many places.

The only face he picked out immediately was Nodoka’s. Mai was next to her. She was doing her braids-and-glasses combo, so no one around had recognized her. Nodoka was attracting all the attention like a lightning rod.

Mai saw Sakuta looking and flashed him a quick smile.

“Ootsu, which would you prefer?”

“Huh?”

“Do you want her watching or not?”

“I want her watching.”

Minagi didn’t hesitate. She might not have raised her head yet, but there was an intensity behind her words—and a soft note on top, reserved for Kaho.

“Then she’s watching.”

“What if I said I didn’t want her watching?”

“She’d also be watching.”

That was how these things worked.

Before they could say anything else, the starting pistol went off.

Two pairs from each color—so six pairs in all—set off around the track. A half lap—the next pair was waiting for the baton around the bend.

“The Three-Legged Race is a relay race?”

“Apparently.”

Worryingly, Minagi was in the same boat he was. She really had slept through the event-selection homeroom.

“Well, we’re at the end of the line, so let’s assume we’re the anchors. We just gotta get the baton and hit the finish line.”

Minagi was shrugging this off, but the Three-Legged Race was near the end of the sports festival—the crowd was way more worked up than Sakuta had expected. This was not an event that depended solely on running skills, so it was hard to predict who’d win—that helped keep it exciting.

The second pair was handing the baton to the third.

That left only the fourth—the anchors. Sakuta and Minagi.

Minagi put her arm round Sakuta’s waist. The sudden grab made him grunt.

“Grab my shoulders,” she said, so he put an arm around hers. Two tight grips, very stable. He could really tell how strong her core was.

“Start with the tied leg, moving one, two, one, two.”

No time to argue. The baton was approaching fast.

“Got it.”

Minagi kept going “One, two, one two” as they moved into the baton pass zone.

The pair coming toward them was Saki and a first-year boy…who was rather red in the face. He must’ve been incredibly embarrassed. They were in fourth place. The pairs behind them had fumbled the baton pass on the second or third round, so they were a solid half lap behind.

“Here!” Saki grumpily handed the baton over, and they caught it.

“And one, two.” They set off. Minagi kept that rhythm going. “One, two, one, two.”

Their pace was much faster than Sakuta had expected. He nearly stumbled. But if he complained or tried to change speeds, they’d immediately tumble to the ground—all he could do was force his feet to stay on beat.

Ahead of them were two red pairs and a yellow one. Halfway around the bend, they passed the third-place yellow pair. They caught up with the second-place pair at the end of the bend and blew by.

Only the first-place pair left.

But even at a low estimate, they had a solid ten-yard lead.

The finish line was right there. Their half lap was almost over. No way to catch up—

Or so he thought, but the lead team crossed the finish line and kept on going, not slowing down at all. As he wondered why, the broadcast-club commentary answered for him.

“The anchor teams get a full lap! This battle’s not over yet!”

But his legs were dead. He’d gone all out on the assumption they only had to run a half lap.

“You got this, Sakuta!” Yuuma yelled from the blue seats. Unnecessary.

“Senpai, move those feet!”

Was that Tomoe?

She didn’t need to tell him. He was moving his feet. Moving them like his life depended on it. That was the only way he could keep up with Minagi.

The crowd was really going wild now. Cheers were coming from all directions, trying to overwhelm him.

They were through the back straight and on the curve again. Then—

“Minagi! Gooooo!” someone yelled.

He felt Minagi jump. She kept chanting “One, two, one, two,” but her eyes were on the stands at the curve.

On a girl in a gray tracksuit. Kaho Hamamatsu.

Minagi didn’t say a word.

But her arm tightened around his waist.

He had an idea what she wanted. He knew, but he argued, “My legs are dead.”

Despite that, Minagi just snorted. Derisively. Her lips curled gleefully, and she upped the pace of her “One, two, one, two.”

And when Sakuta started to drag behind, her firm grip on his waist pulled him right along.

Three yards to the lead pair. Ten to the goalposts.

At this point, his mind went blank. He couldn’t breathe. His legs felt like lead. The grip on his waist allowed no escape; he was joined to Minagi at the hip.

All he could think about was not falling, and that kept both legs pumping.

They were almost at the finish line.

They were neck and neck with the other pair now. He could almost feel their looks of surprise on his skin. And then they took their last steps.

The finish tape hit Sakuta’s and Minagi’s hips, and they soared across the line, running for a solid twenty yards past it.

They gradually slowed down until finally coming to a halt straight off the track—they hadn’t taken the curve.

The moment they stopped, Sakuta collapsed. He’d never been more out of breath. He’d have liked to grumble but was in no state to speak. His body demanded oxygen.

Meanwhile, Minagi only needed a couple of deep breaths. She had her hands on her hips, standing straight and tall. Here was a true athlete. Kinda cool. Downright badass, even.

Ever since she’d stopped, Minagi’s eyes had been on one thing. On the far corner, where Kaho had been.

The crowds were still buzzing from Sakuta and Minagi’s come-from-behind victory; students were on their feet and jumping around. Sakuta couldn’t find Kaho in the chaos.

But Minagi must have—her eyes were locked on a single point and not budging. Sakuta followed her gaze, and after a minute, Kaho emerged from the Minegahara crowd. She ran toward them, but pulled up short a good ten yards out.

Kaho seemed nervous.

Sakuta wordlessly untied the knot on their feet.

“Kaho,” Minagi said, running over to her. He thought that would be it, but she stopped halfway, turning back to Sakuta. “Thanks, Azusagawa.”

“You’re welcome.”

“Will you take payment in boobs or butt?”

“Got my fill of both during this race,” he said, getting up. “Go on, get,” he said, waving her toward Kaho. The rest was their problem.

“Thanks,” Minagi said again, and then she ran the rest of the way to Kaho, light on her feet.

Sakuta’s feet were deadweights, but he dragged them back toward the school. He was going to rest in class until the sports festival was done and over, no matter what.

13

He had no idea what Minagi and Kaho said to each other, or what resolution they reached. That was for the two of them to know.

What mattered to Sakuta was that Minagi showed up for the Relay Race, as planned.

She was the third runner and got the baton in last place—she passed the red and yellow teams and handed the baton to the anchor in first. They kept the lead she’d made, and the blue team finished first.

That put their total score ahead of the red and yellow teams, and they won the entire sports festival.

It wasn’t every day that a sports festival was so close that the outcome of the final event could settle everything, so it had been well worth watching. The students were so wound up they were reluctant to head home; there were still tons of them hanging around school even after the closing ceremony.

Sakuta had been the first person back in the classroom, and he wasted no time changing and getting ready to leave. Oblivious to the lingering excitement around him, he headed right for the shoe lockers.

Mai and Nodoka had left ahead of him, so he was on his own.

She’d made lunch for him, and they’d searched for Minagi together… It might not have been a traditional sports festival experience, but he was glad to have spent that time with Mai.

With that thought on his mind, he opened his shoe locker and found a note inside.

“What’s this?” he wondered, unfolding it.

Have fun with the Three-Legged Race?

It was in Mai’s neat handwriting.

He stuffed it in the pocket of his uniform.

“I wish I could do a Three-Legged Race with Mai.”

Dreaming about that, he headed home ahead of the rest of the school.

Naturally, he spent the next day racked with muscle pains.

chapters.text: Rascal Does Not Dream of a Beach Queen, Vol. 16

chapters.title: Rascal Does Not Dream of a Beach Queen, Vol. 16
chapters.text:
Rascal Does Not Dream of a Beach Queen, Vol. 16

He’d long felt like he was forgetting something vital.

Something he remembered in his dreams that slipped away come morning.

He’d wake up emotional, for reasons he couldn’t figure out.

But it felt important.

He knew this mattered.

Even if he didn’t know what it was.

He hoped he’d figure it out someday, and life went on.

And once more—Christmas came around.

1

That morning, Sakuta Azusagawa was woken by her kiss.

He’d felt her crawl into his bed, and he’d known it must be morning. But his eyes failed to open. She wriggled into the loose sweatshirt he slept in, moved up his stomach to his chest and then out the neck—and finally licked his cheek.

“Five more minutes…,” he muttered, half asleep.

Her answer was another kiss. Well, more of a slurp.

That was impossible to sleep through.

Sakuta gave up and forced his heavy eyelids open.

Before his eyes was the head of a tricolored cat, sticking out of his sweatshirt.

“Meow,” she said, in a rather low voice for a lady cat. Her name was Nasuno.

“Morning, Nasuno.”

“Mew.”

Sakuta turned his eyes toward his alarm clock. It was 6:59 AM…and then it flipped to seven. The alarm started blaring, but he stopped it instantly. The arm that had slipped outside his covers was freezing already.

It was winter. December 24. Christmas Eve.

He was feeling very ready for winter vacation, but sadly, they still had school today. The last day of the second term, which was the day of the end-of-term ceremony.

It would hardly be a big deal if he skipped that. It’d be awfully nice to sleep in, tucked in his warm bed. The ultimate winter luxury.

But not today.

“Better get up.”

Sakuta won the battle quick, despite the chilly room.

“Too cold…”

It was extra nippy this morning.

“I guess they were predicting snow…”

He’d half watched the weather report last night, and there’d been a big cold front moving in. They’d been expecting accumulation in the flat and coastal areas of Kanto. “I’m sure a lot of people will be venturing out for Christmas Eve, but please do watch your step,” the weather lady said.

Last year, Sakuta had no such plans and would have resented the implication, but this year, he was nodding along. I will watch my step, he’d thought. This year, he had plenty of plans.

He pulled Nasuno out of his clothes.

“Mrow,” she said, clearly hungry. He followed her into the living room.

First, he put some kibble in her bowl.

The sound of her crunching away filled the quiet room.

This morning, only Nasuno and Sakuta were home.

Their dad had picked Kaede up just after noon yesterday, and she was spending the night at their grandparents’. They were probably doting on her right that second. It had been a solid two years since they’d seen her…

She wouldn’t be home until the day after tomorrow, the twenty-sixth.

“Stay as long as you like,” he’d told her when she was leaving.

“I’ll be back the twenty-sixth,” Kaede insisted.

She was dead set on that, her glare making it clear he couldn’t change her mind.

He could guess why.

Kaede had things to do when she got back.

Sakuta put a slice of bread in the toaster and fried an egg in the meantime.

Once both were done, he scarfed them down.

He washed the pan and was putting it away when the phone rang.

The number on-screen was his dad’s cell.

He dried his hands, picked up the receiver, and said, “Hello?”

“Oh, Sakuta?” Far too cute a voice to be his dad.

Clearly, this was not his dad but his sister, Kaede.

“What?”

“What do you mean, what?”

He’d just asked, but she got mad at him for it.

“You called me.”

“I didn’t call when I arrived yesterday, so I am now.”

She must have been talking about their grandparents’ house.

“Are Grandma and Grandpa doing okay?”

“They’re good. They wish you came along.”

“I’ll go over eventually. Now go get spoiled enough for both of us.”

“Then I get your Christmas presents and New Year’s money, right?”

How greedy.

“I’ve got Mai, so I can let you have that much.”

Mai had agreed to a date today. They’d be meeting up at six, after she got off work. Given how packed her schedule was, getting to spend Christmas together was a real blessing.

That promise was the only thing that convinced him to get out of bed that morning and go to school instead of sleeping in.

“Mai doesn’t like it when you’re rude.”

It was Christmas. Sakuta would love to do quite a few “rude” things with Mai. As much as he could get away with, no matter what it took to get him there. But telling his sister this would hardly be appropriate, so he held his tongue.

“Actually, Mai thought you’d be here. She suggested we all have cake together.”

“I would be such a third wheel. That’s why I’m here.”

“My Mai would never think that.”

“But you totally would,” Kaede huffed. She didn’t even bother hiding how put out she was.

“Don’t sweat it. Toyohama swears she’s coming right back home after her Christmas concert, so you’d be more of a fourth wheel.”

The third wheel would have dazzling blond hair.

“I’m gonna tell Nodoka you said that.”

“No need, I’ll tell her myself.”

He needed to get that siscon idol to back off a bit.

“……You’re one weird dude,” Kaede muttered.

“I gotta get ready for school. Hanging up.”

“Oh, sorry, wait!”

“Mm? What?”

“Um, er…” Kaede’s voice dwindled away.

“……”

Sakuta said nothing, waiting for her to finish.

“So, uh…”

Even over the phone, he could tell she had something on her mind. It must’ve been really hard for her to say. And that gave Sakuta a good idea what it must be.

“Um, once I get back…”

She’d started big, but her voice dropped to a whisper.

“You need help practicing the walk to school?”

“Why’d you say it for me?!”

He figured she looked as peeved as she sounded. He bet she was pouting so hard her lips stuck out.

“ ’Cause it’s time for me to go.”

He actually had a few minutes to spare, but these types of family discussions made him uncomfortable. Like an itch he couldn’t scratch.

“……Thanks, Sakuta.”

“Hanging up now.”

“Mm, okay.”

She seemed ready to drag this discomfort out, so he wrapped things up.

Nasuno had finished eating and let out a satisfied meow. She began washing her face and scratching the back of her neck with her hind legs.

Looking up from the cat, Sakuta realized Kaede had left her bedroom door open. Her junior high uniform was on a hanger by the closet. She must have gotten it ready before she left yesterday. So the moment she got home, she could put it on and walk to school. So she could go to school every day.

Nasuno meowed again.

It was high time Sakuta got changed and left.

2

Leaving Nasuno to guard the fort, Sakuta left just before eight.

Outside the front door, the cold air pricked his skin. Just inhaling sent a chill up his nose; his breath was more visible than any day so far this season.

If he asked Rio why he could see his breath, she’d likely give him a scientific explanation. He’d have to bring it up if he saw her today. But by then, he’d have clean forgotten his question.

With that, he set off for Fujisawa Station.

After ten minutes on foot, he saw it up ahead. The station looked like it always did. Even on December 24, the morning rush was just another weekday. Men in suits and ties poured through the gates. College students yawned. Quite a few younger students were in their uniforms.

Sakuta was but one of many.

He cut across the station interior from the north to the south exit. The Odakyu Department Store loomed up ahead, and he moved to the Enoden Fujisawa Station platform beside it and boarded a waiting train.

It slowly pulled out, the green-and-cream retro carriage rocking for a good fifteen minutes, running along the coast to Shichirigahama Station.

Everyone in Minegahara uniforms got out here, forming a line where the ticket machine stood at attention since this station had no gate with turnstiles.

Sakuta tapped his card and stepped outside. The school was right up ahead.

He heard the girls in front of him talking.

“It’s too cold today.”

“Super cold.”

“Crazy cold.”

They were laughing happily. There might be snow coming, but their skirts were still above their knees, bare legs beneath. Just looking at them made Sakuta cold, so he turned his eyes to the sky.

Thin clouds covered it in a dull gray.

He could just about locate the sun’s position, but not much light was making it through. A very wintry sky. Even if he hadn’t seen the weather report, his skin told him snow was coming. The air already smelled like it. Maybe farther from the coast, it was already coming down.

But if it was gonna snow, let it snow.

Sakuta would prefer if it didn’t come down bad enough to stop the trains, but he was wasn’t about to cancel a Christmas date with Mai over a few flakes. The cold just gave him more chances to cuddle. He’d take any excuse he could get. His excitement was steadily rising.

“It’s too cold today.”

“Super cold.”

“Crazy cold.”

The exact same exchange he’d just heard, but this time, it was behind him. Sakuta hurried on to the school entrance, dreaming of today’s date.

The end-of-term ceremony wrapped up way faster than expected. It was primarily because the principal kept his remarks brief, citing the cold. Sakuta vaguely remembered him saying something like “As the temperatures dip below freezing, third-years with exams looming must take care not to catch a cold and stay the course.”

In the homeroom that followed, report cards were handed out; his grades were not bad. They were quite decent, actually. A solid rank higher than his first-term results. He gave all the credit to Mai’s tutoring.

There was a chance this could help him score a delightful reward on their date. His excitement rose again—he was on the verge of humming.

The class was still buzzing when he left, floating on wings of anticipation.

He made it all the way to the shoe lockers without speaking to anyone, changed shoes, and stepped outside.

He went through the school gates and over the Enoden crossing. He took a moment to appreciate the view of the Shichirigahama waters, then he turned right and headed to the station.

Most students were still lingering in the classroom. Sakuta had ditched the moment homeroom ended, so the platform was still mostly empty.

Maybe four or five other students.

A distinctive hush had fallen over the station.

As he was waiting for the train at the end of the platform, someone called out, “Ah, Senpai!”

He turned his head and found a petite high schooler with a scarf wrapped around her. The tip of her nose was red, her breath white. It was Tomoe Koga, a student one year below him.

“On your own today?” he asked.

When he ran into her at the station after school, she was usually with her friend Nana Yoneyama.

“Nana’s on cleaning duty,” she said, joining him. “And I’ve got a shift today. You’re working, too, right? So I’m not being a loner.”

She was speaking very fast, like he’d accused her of something.

“You’re on your own, Senpai?”

“Well, I’m with you now, Koga.”

“I meant not with Sakurajima.”

She shot him a dirty look. It said, “I know you knew that; why you gotta be that way?”

“Mai’s working, so she wasn’t at school today.”

She had a shoot at the TV studio this morning.

“Aha,” Tomoe said, looking relieved. She’d had one eye on their surroundings, worried that she might be interrupting his rendezvous with Mai.

“Don’t worry, we’ve got a date planned after my shift.”

“I wasn’t worried! Don’t boast about it! You’re terribad!”

“You?”

“Puh-leez, I don’t have any wonderful boyfriends to spend Christmas with.”

Tomoe snorted, making a show of turning her back on him. She even crossed her arms to better fume.

“No plans with friends?”

“At the moment, just dinner with family and a cake,” she reluctantly admitted.

“Aha.”

“And tomorrow I’m going out for pancakes with Nana and some friends.”

Her lips were still jutting out.

“Well, sounds like you’ve got a great Christmas planned.”

“Do I?”

“You’re spending it with your wonderful family and friends.”

Sakuta didn’t think time spent with them was in any way inferior. He hadn’t made time for family since he started living away from his parents. It may have simply been a standard annual celebration for Tomoe, but Sakuta thought having a tradition like that was arguably the definition of happiness. It was just too normal for her to realize how lucky she was.

“Well, just don’t overeat and regret it later.”

“I’ll be dieting the rest of winter break, so I’ll break even.”

Tomoe flashed him a triumphant smile.

But what she’d said was not remotely reassuring.

“I hope that diet works out this time.”

“What’s that supposed to mean?”

“I feel like this is the fifth or sixth time you’ve told me you’re going on a diet.”

“And they mostly work out!”

“Do they?”

From how she acted, it really didn’t seem like they had. Not that she was particularly overweight to begin with…

“I usually aim to lose six pounds, and manage to lose four!”

Those numbers weren’t exactly awe-inspiring.

“Aren’t you gaining like two pounds with each diet? After repeating that five or six times…”

“Augh! I have not gained ten pounds! There’s no way!”

Tomoe had gone bright red, vehemently denying it. She waved her hands around as she insisted, “I haven’t!”

“Koga, you don’t really need to force yourself to lose weight.”

“Why not?”

“You don’t look fat.”

He’d thought that for a while now and had said as much on more than one occasion, but Tomoe never seemed to listen. She didn’t get it. Men and women seemed to have different definitions of overweight, and he’d found no way to bridge that gap.

“You wouldn’t know. You’ve never seen me,” Tomoe said with a baleful glare. She was rubbing her tummy.

“I’ve seen you at the beach.”

“In a swimsuit! Also, forget that ever happened.”

“How can I forget your butt bulwark?”

They’d made sandcastles at the edge of the surf, competing to see which could last against the waves the longest. Sakuta lost. Tomoe’s castle had been protected by a deep, wide moat in the shape of a butt, sapping the strength of the incoming waves. Three matches had ended in three losses. Total defeat.

“Augh, why did I ever go to the beach with you?” Tomoe crouched down, clutching her head. “I could never put a swimsuit on with you around! I must have been out of my mind.”

She was muttering away, lamenting her life choices.

“You two headed home?” a voice jumped in. “You seem like you’re having fun.”

It was Yuuma Kunimi, Sakuta’s friend and a coworker at the same restaurant.

“Well, Koga—,” Sakuta began.

“Augh! Augh!” Tomoe was back on her feet, cutting him off. She got up in his face, yelling every time he tried to say anything, jumping up and down. “Why would you ever tell him?! I can’t trust you farther than I can throw you!”

“Kunimi asked.”

“Don’t blame him!”

“No secrets between friends.”

“Don’t blab people’s secrets!”

“……?”

Yuuma had no idea what this was about and looked baffled.

“Look, the train’s coming!” Tomoe said, forcing them off topic. “You’ve got a shift today, Kunimi?”

“Looks like we all do.”

They boarded the train, chatting about nothing.

By the time they got to Fujisawa, the conversation had drifted to how old they were when they stopped believing in Santa.

“I’d just started grade school.”

“Same. Sakuta?”

“I still believe. I’m planning on becoming Santa Claus someday.”

“If you only work on Christmas, you would just be Sakurajima’s kept man.”

Tomoe and Yuuma both gave him a look of deep pity. What for?

3

“It’s snowing pretty hard,” Yuuma said as he came through the back door of the restaurant. He’d been taking the trash out.

“I can see that.”

There were several flakes on Yuuma’s head and the shoulders of his waiter uniform.

“I bet it actually sticks.”

“Yep.”

This exchange happened just past two, right as the lunch rush was dying down.

The snow kept falling, and by the time Sakuta got off at five, the roads around Fujisawa Station were turning white.

“Thanks. I’m outta here,” he told the manager, then was out the door.

Nightfall had made it even colder, and he shriveled up against the wind. The cars in the lot had snow on their hoods.

“I hope Mai’s okay.”

Traffic was still flowing smoothly according to Tomoe, who’d checked her phone in the break room as they got ready to leave. But if it kept coming down like this, there was no telling. The area around the restaurant was still seeing a lot of cars and foot traffic, but the snow was starting to pile up in earnest.

In a city that didn’t get much snow, that could shut everything down.

“Well, if Mai’s late, I’ll just get her to do something to make up for it.”

This could turn into a very good Christmas for Sakuta. With that in mind, he opened the plastic umbrella he’d borrowed from the restaurant and set off.

He had a full hour until they’d agreed to meet, so he planned to stop by home first. He’d gone straight from school to work and was still in uniform, and Nasuno would be getting hungry.

Back at the station proper, he took the stairs to the overpass. Work and his apartment building were on opposite sides of the station.

The overpass had quite a bit of snow on it. He could still see the tiles where foot traffic was heavy, but the edges were white.

Minding his step through the station, he nearly bumped into someone coming out of the Bic Camera. He’d been too focused on the wet footing to watch where he was going.

“Oh, sorry,” he said, glancing up at a girl carrying a bag from the Junkudo Bookstore.

She seemed familiar, but for a moment, he couldn’t place her. She made a face and averted her eyes. That gesture was all he needed to know it was Rio.

She was so different he hadn’t recognized her right away. Her hair and clothes were a big departure from what Rio was usually like.

She was wearing a pretty nice dress under a coat with a fur-like trim. The skirts went to her knees, spreading out like the letter A. Black tights and glossy shoes with a bit of a heel rounded out her outfit.

She had her hair up and a bit to one side.

It was a much more grown-up look, a touch of elegance.

Was it a special occasion? She seemed like she was headed to the kind of restaurant that served food in courses.

“……”

Sakuta shot her a look, demanding an explanation, but Rio said nothing. So he started with a simple question.

“Shopping?”

His gaze dropped to the bag in her hand. More incomprehensible physics tomes? Highly likely. The seventh and eighth floors of the Bic Camera building were a massive bookstore that could rival any library. They had a good selection of specialized texts.

“I thought you had a date, Azusagawa,” she said, shifting the subject.

“We’re going to the aquarium.”

They were meeting up just outside the gates of Katase-Enoshima Station.

“I didn’t ask.”

Rio was still refusing to meet his eye. She seemed highly uncomfortable. She was probably hoping with all her heart for him to just go away.

Sakuta was fully aware of that and didn’t let it get him down; he was too busy taking in Rio’s unusual outfit. At length, she let out a very long sigh.

“I’m going out for dinner with my parents in Minato Mirai,” she said, answering his unspoken question. She seemed very reluctant—not to go out with her parents, but to have to explain this to Sakuta.

“You’ve mentioned before they’re super busy.”

“They both had a sudden cancellation today. When I got home from school, they were both there. It’s been years since they had a moment like this, so before I knew it, we made plans to go out.”

Rio had told him her dad worked at a big college hospital and spent a lot of his time caught up in office politics.

Her mother worked in fashion and spent half the year abroad on business.

As a result, they almost never ate together.

Her hesitance was likely a by-product of that.

“My mom picked these clothes, and the hair… She booked an appointment at a beauty salon, and they did this to me.”

“Well, you look great.”

She looked all grown-up. Not in a “suddenly sexy” way, but in a mature, sophisticated way. But there was still a trace of a teen trying to act grown-up—he could tell her mom really understood Rio’s appeal.

Previously, Rio had insisted her parents just weren’t interested in her, but maybe they were seeing what mattered.

“Not by choice,” she said, extra emphatic.

Clearly, this was the main point she wanted Sakuta to take away. She’d given him the full version of her night’s plans just to drive that home.

It was very Rio to give a step-by-step briefing just for that.

“Futaba.”

“What?” she asked, guarded.

“Can I borrow your phone?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Knowing you, you’ll take a picture of me and send it to Kunimi.”

“Am I that obvious?”

She had him dead to rights. It was nice to have friends who understood you.

It was anyone’s guess how long it’d be before he got another chance to see her in formal wear; he’d have loved to preserve it for posterity, but not if she was that against it.

“Wish I hadn’t taken this detour. I could’ve avoided you entirely.”

“Well, I got a feast for the eyes.”

“Azusagawa, you know you only have eyes for Sakurajima.”

“I bet Mai would look amazing all dressed up.”

“You’ll get to see her all dressed up in white someday. If she doesn’t throw you out first, that is.”

“I plan to see that from the best seat in the house.”

Rio obviously meant a wedding dress. When he tried to picture Mai in a wedding gown…a wave of powerful emotion washed over him.

“……?”

For a second, he saw a woman in a wedding dress. From her height alone, he knew it wasn’t Mai, but that was the only thing he knew for certain. Her face was a blur, her outline hazy. He felt like her lips had moved, but he couldn’t make out the words. Couldn’t hear her voice. And when he tried to focus on her, the image melted away.

The emotions that bubbled up kept roiling inside him.

It felt like he’d forgotten something vital.

Like he was trying to remember and failing.

But accompanied by a strange sort of warmth.

Led by that emotion, he found his hand on his chest.

“……”

“Azusagawa? What’s wrong?”

Sakuta’s sudden silence left Rio peering at his face, concerned.

“Uh…nothing,” he said, as if trying to convince himself. He lowered his hand. This was hardly the first time he’d felt something like this; it had happened several times before. Especially since they moved to Fujisawa.

But no matter how many times it happened, he couldn’t work out what it meant. And still hadn’t.

“Oh? Well, fine.”

Rio pulled her phone out of her purse. It must have buzzed. She checked the screen and sent a reply. Probably one of her parents. Maybe they were here to pick her up.

“Oh, Azusagawa…”

“Mm?”

“Sakurajima’s voicing the announcements inside.”

Rio jerked her thumb at the entrance to Bic Camera. Even at this distance, they could just make out her voice.

“I know. Already gave them a listen.”

“You would.”

“And I’m gonna hear plenty more face-to-face later on.”

“You really are a rascal, Azusagawa.”

With that, Rio put her phone away.

“My dad’s car is here. Gotta run.”

She glanced at the road at the bottom of the stairs. A car had pulled up, hazard lights flashing. It was German. Even Sakuta knew that brand. The passenger window opened, and a woman in sunglasses leaned out. She waved at Rio.

“Go have fun,” he said.

Rio hesitated a second, her gaze dropping. But she soon looked up.

“Try not to do anything too crazy, Azusagawa.”

Her smile looked like she’d ironed out some things and left her worries behind.

Her watched her go down the stairs and slide into the back seat of the car. The door closed, and the car pulled away. Watching the taillights fade into the distance, he muttered, “Futaba really is a rich girl,” as if it had only just sunk in.

4

After Rio left, Sakuta hurried home through the flurries. He’d worked till five and had to be at the date spot by six. Since he’d stopped to chat with Rio, he had very little time to spare.

He reached home at 5:25.

“Mrow!”

Nasuno met him at the door, and the first thing he did was pour some food in her bowl.

Then he moved to his room and cast off his uniform. For a moment, he was wearing nothing but his socks. He put on some new underwear, pants, and a T-shirt, then a sweater over that. Finally, he put on his coat and said “Mind the fort, Nasuno” on his way back out.

Nasuno was too busy crunching to answer, so he left the house without farewells.

He traced his path back to Fujisawa Station. The snow wasn’t going anywhere; if anything, it was coming down harder.

The wind was picking up, and snow was streaming by. It was hard to block it all with a single umbrella, and flakes were catching on him from the waist down. If he didn’t brush them off from time to time, his pants would have turned white.

In these conditions, it took him longer to reach the station than he’d expected.

He’d still be there on time, but Mai was famous; best not to leave her waiting. He’d wanted to be there ahead of time.

Sakuta stepped onto the Odakyu Enoshima Line platform and found the 5:41 to Katase-Enoshima sounding the warning bell.

“Let me on!”

He jumped onto the train. The last car.

The doors slammed shut behind him, and the train sped off. Near Fujisawa Station there were office buildings and towering apartments, but that soon gave way to a quiet residential area. The roofs along the tracks were all covered in white, turning the familiar view into a winter wonderland.

Sakuta took in those sights out of the corner of his eye as he moved down the train. Katase-Enoshima Station was the end of the line, and the gates were at the head of the train.

The snow did not affect the train’s progress. It stopped at Hon-Kugenuma and Kugenuma Beach before reaching Katase-Enoshima at 5:48, as scheduled.

He waited for the doors to open and disembarked. Umbrella flowers bloomed all around him, and only then did he realize how many other passengers were on the train. Maybe half of them were couples. Lots of girls slipped under their boyfriend’s umbrella.

The weather couldn’t ruin a date night. Everyone seemed to be enjoying the snow. Especially today. Christmas Eve plus snow equaled fun date. The whole station seemed positively giddy.

That vibe continued beyond the gates as well.

The clearing outside the station was now a spot for couples to meet up. At a glance, there were thirty or forty milling about. All young men and women around twenty, give or take a few years; all waiting for their partners to arrive.

Some were waiting and smiling at the crowd streaming from the gates, even running up to each other and sliding in the snow.

Others were stuck to their phones, waiting for the next train.

Assuming he’d have to join the waiting crowd, Sakuta opened his umbrella and took a step away from the Dragon Palace–styled station.

Would Mai be on the next train? Only one other train would arrive before six, so it seemed likely. Hard to imagine her ever being late.

That was a solid seven-minute wait. He’d planned to just stare into space, but those plans were soon dashed—because he saw the person he’d been waiting for.

“Ah,” he squeaked.

Mai was in the crowd just outside the gates, umbrella overhead.

She was wearing a slim-cut down coat and a baggy sweater. Below that she wore skinny slacks and boots—for safety in the snow. To avoid anyone recognizing Mai Sakurajima, she had a newsboy cap pulled down low and a pair of fake glasses with stylish round frames. Her hair was loosely braided, and she had a scarf wrapped fairly high, but in a natural way.

The whole ensemble screamed college girl.

It was a departure from how she usually looked in movies, TV shows, or fashion magazines; no one had recognized her. No one was even giving her a second glance. Everyone was focused on their texts with the person they were here to meet.

As Sakuta stared at Mai, her eyes flicked his way.

They met.

But Mai looked away as if nothing had happened. She pulled a phone out of her coat pocket and fiddled with it. The bunny-eared cover was the same one Mai used.

Sakuta stepped over to her and said “What’s the big idea, Mai?” in a soft voice.

She stopped fiddling with the phone and looked back at him, like he’d spoiled the fun.

“I thought it would take you longer to spot me,” she grumbled, sighing. “Nobody else noticed the whole way here.”

She then showed off her disguise proudly. “Well?”

“It’s a date, but you’re not in a skirt. Disappointing.”

That was his honest opinion.

“You’d rather your cute girlfriend be cold?” Mai said, even more put out.

“I’d warm y—”

Before he could finish, Mai’s boot found his foot.

“Anything else to say for yourself ?”

“I love you.”

“Not that.”

“I really love you.”

“……”

Mai narrowed her eyes.

“My Mai is the cutest girl around.”

“But you’re unhappy about the skirt.”

“You’ve convinced me to wait until spring. I know you’ll reward my patience.”

“Yes, fine, I’ll wear a skirt to a date once it warms up.”

“Bare legs?”

“Never. I don’t want to tan.”

“I’ll put the sunscreen on you.”

“That’s even worse.”

“Aww.”

“Why did you think I’d go for that?”

It would save Mai from the dreaded tan. Sakuta would get to see and feel her bare legs. That was the definition of a win-win.

“All right, come on.”

Mai cut the conversation off, closing her umbrella and slipping under Sakuta’s. She wrapped her arm around his. Since she was tall, that put her face right next to his.

“……”

“What?”

She shot him a look, daring him to grumble.

“If only you were wearing less.”

They were both wearing winter coats. With all that padding, he couldn’t feel anything pressing up against his arm.

“Don’t be stupid. We’re going to the aquarium.”

Mai nudged him, and they set off through the snow. The road leading south from the station was full of couples headed to the beach or coming back from it.

“Tell me, Sakuta.”

“Tell you what?”

“How’d you know it was me?”

Mai must have been very confident in that disguise. She wasn’t letting it go. Perhaps she’d planned to make fun of him all night for not spotting her and was put out that her plans had been dashed.

“I guess it’s just because you’re always on my mind.”

He couldn’t think of anything else.

“You have better things to think about.”

“For instance?”

“Say…your future?” Mai suggested, after a moment’s thought.

“When we get married, I’d like you to call me ‘darling.’ ”

That was the first “future” that sprang to mind.

“I’m not marrying a professional Santa Claus.”

“Aww.”

That was a wonderful job. It gave children happy dreams.

Still, he’d said that off-the-cuff, and he was surprised she’d remembered it.

“I could be a reindeer?”

“You would like getting whipped, Sakuta.”

“Only if it’s you giving me some tough love, Mai.”

“In that case, I’ll give you more studying assignments tomorrow. You have to get into the same college as me, don’t you?”

Mai smirked at him. Clearly, he’d gotten carried away and said too much. Best to get the subject back on track before she made him commit to anything.

“Would you rather I hadn’t figured it out?”

“Mm?”

“Your disguise.”

They got caught at a red light on Route 134. The coastal highway was full of speeding cars.

Sakuta had nothing better to do while they waited for the walk light, so he looked at Mai instead. She was looking at him.

“I was glad you did. Of course,” she admitted. She turned her head down, burying half her face in the scarf. She seemed pleased, embarrassed—and tickled. It all mingled into one happy expression.

And getting to see that up close made Sakuta just as happy. A jolt of joy shot through him.

“Um, Mai.”

“Wh-what?”

“Can I hug you?”

“Once we’re home.”

“Oh? Really?”

He’d assumed she’d say no.

“But no more than a hug.”

His joy was cut short.

“But I even changed my underwear.”

“All the more reason not to, then,” Mai said with a withering look.

“Can’t we get swept up in the moment and kiss?”

“Nodoka said she’d be coming right back after her concert, so…restrain yourself today.”

“I hope the snow keeps coming and the trains stop running.”

Nodoka’s Christmas concert was at a venue in the city, so she’d be stuck there overnight.

If that happened, once they got back from their date, Sakuta would have all Mai’s cooking to himself. And Mai to himself.

“She swore she’d make it back, so she will make it back.” Mai chuckled, clearly remembering Nodoka’s ferocity.

“Toyohama really needs to learn to let go.”

The light turned green.

The crowd on the corner was on the move.

Sakuta and Mai matched pace with the couple in front of them.

A second crowd was approaching from the opposite side of the intersection. The two streams passed each other in the center of the street. Sakuta spotted a red umbrella in the oncoming flow, carried by a young girl—judging from her clothing, she was in junior high. The umbrella hid her face, but she was laughing happily, talking to her parents.

At first, she just caught his eye.

But as they hit the far sidewalk, his body turned on its own, doing an about-face.

The red umbrella was already lost in the crowd.

“Something wrong?” Mai asked.

“There was a girl with a red umbrella…”

That was all he managed. When he tried to explain why he cared, he couldn’t find a reason.

“You know her?”

“Well, not exactly…,” he said vaguely.

“Did your first love carry a red umbrella?” Mai asked, teasing him.

“I think I’d remember that.”

But what else could it be? Pondering that, they moved on. They could see the new Enoshima Aquarium up ahead.

He was still thinking about red umbrellas when he felt a pinch on his cheek.

It was Mai.

He didn’t have to ask why. She was rebuking him for letting his mind wander on their date.

“Jealous, Mai?”

“Yes.”

Mouthing off earned him a harder pinch.

“Owww.”

“That was the wrong answer.”

“I’m sorry!”

Best to concede this one. Mai let go of his cheek. Then she put her arms around Sakuta’s again—tighter this time. Like she wasn’t letting him go.

“I’m blessed to have you as my girlfriend.”

He was beaming at her.

“Don’t be dramatic.”

“You’re making me.”

“Do you want me to let go?”

“I want to stay like this forever.”

He’d made his intentions clear, but Mai let go of him the moment they reached the aquarium. She got in line for the counter and came back with two tickets.

“Did you not hear what I said, Mai?”

“If it’s still snowing on the way home, I’ll get under your umbrella again.”

“In that case, we could rain check the aquarium and keep walking around.”

“I already bought the tickets.”

Mai headed for the doors, almost skipping. She was obviously having a good time.

“You really like aquariums?” Sakuta asked, catching up.

“I do. Especially if you’re with me.” She took his hand.

If she put it that way, he had no choice but to tour the aquarium with her.

His head was full of Mai again, so for now, he focused on their time together.

5

As they followed the route through the aquarium, they turned a corner and found themselves in another world.

The entrance staircase leading to the second floor had fantastical images of swimming sea turtles projected onto it, and the visitors were letting out squeals of delight.

It felt like walking through the ocean.

And not far past the top of the stairs, they began seeing living sea creatures. The exhibit started with a display about cultivating whitebait, and while they were reading that, a giant ray swam by overhead. The ray tank formed the ceiling of this corridor. From below, they could clearly see the smiling face on the ray’s underside. Lots of couples were aiming their phones its way.

The passage sloped gently downward. Back on the first floor, the view opened up before a massive tank. This was full of fish that lived in the Sagami Bay. At the center of it, a school of several thousand sardines were dancing in sync.

Once more, every couple brandished their phones. No shutter sounds. They must have been taking videos. A little boy here with his family was pointing excitedly and yelling, “Sharks! There’s a shark!”

Beyond the big tank were deep-sea creatures—the kind you see on TV a lot—and a display of colorful tropical fish.

Every section was packed with couples gazing happily at the marine life and taking photos.

The most popular exhibit by far was the jellyfish.

The whole area was lit by a blue-and-purple glow, and the jellyfish themselves caught the light like a holiday illumination. But their unpredictable bobbing had a very different appeal than the steadier lights outside.

Until Sakuta actually saw them, he’d been going, “Who goes to look at jellyfish on Christmas?” but he now felt that these creatures were perfect for the season.

The jellyfish probably didn’t give a fig about the holiday, but lit up like this, they were very festive indeed.

Now he understood why the aquarium ads on the Enoden had been hyping up this exhibit.

Mai was taking pictures of the jellyfish, looking thoroughly pleased.

The route took them back up to the second floor, where they watched penguins waddling about and seals doing laps in the pool.

Two of the otters were chasing each other around in the hammock, while two others were doing the same thing in a cage. Everyone watching thought they were adorable.

The crowds were growing, so Sakuta and Mai ceded their spot to a new couple and moved to the next area.

There, they found a dazed-looking capybara.

“He reminds me of you, Sakuta.”

“Does he?”

“But his eyes are far more alive.”

“……”

The capybara was munching on some grass and never once took the slightest interest in Sakuta. Sakuta returned that exact same gaze.

And with that, they left the aquarium.

Everyone had been so focused on their own dates they never realized Mai Sakurajima was there with them. Perhaps that was why Mai grumbled, “Seriously, how did you know?” on the way out the door.

Obviously, no one would expect to see the Mai Sakurajima out on a date in public. He felt like anyone who knew she’d be here would have spotted her just fine.

“What time is it, Mai?”

“Almost seven thirty,” she said, checking her phone.

“What should we do next?”

She had plans to cook for him once they got home, but he had an urge to linger.

For now, he put the umbrella up, and they slowly made their way toward the station. Mai got under his umbrella like she belonged there.

The sidewalk along Route 134 was like a parade of couples leaving the aquarium. And that flow split in two at the walk light up ahead.

Half of them turned to cross the street and return to the station.

The other half was going straight on to Enoshima.

Enoshima had a fancy illumination in the winter and was all lit up; they had a good view of it on the path back from the aquarium.

The Sea Candle rose up like a lighthouse and was shifting from blue to purple. In the snow, that was an especially mystical sight.

“Wanna hit up Enoshima?”

“Maybe next year. I’ll have no time to cook if we do.”

“Then maybe after the New Year’s shrine visit.”

The illumination ran until early February.

“I meant next Christmas.”

He’d been well aware, and Mai knew he was. That’s why she was rolling her eyes at him. They were enjoying their usual banter.

When they reached the light, it had just turned green.

He made to turn toward the station, but Mai tugged his sleeve. “This way, Sakuta,” she said, and they kept going down Route 134. This way led to Enoshima.

“I thought we were saving it for next year.”

They passed the Fujisawa Tourism Center. There were posters for a movie starring Mai outside.

“I thought we’d take the long way around. Just for you, Sakuta. We can take the Enoden back.”

The closest station was Katase-Enoshima Station, on the Odakyu Enoshima Line. But if they walked a little farther, they’d reach the Enoden Enoshima Station—like Mai said, the long way home. But since they’d spend that much more time sharing an umbrella, Sakuta wholeheartedly approved.

They crossed the bridge over the Sakai River together, right where it flowed into the ocean. The wind was cold, and Mai moved even closer to him. Sakuta acted as a shield.

Halfway across the bridge, they saw a light that wasn’t a part of the illumination. It was the red spinning lights of a cop car, stopped just at the end of the bridge, across the street from them.

“Something happen?”

“Maybe.”

They drew closer and could soon see four or five uniformed officers at the end of the Benten Bridge to Enoshima. Next to the cop car was a minivan with the front smashed in, loaded onto a flatbed tow truck.

“Looks like an accident.”

“Yep.”

One of the cops was talking to a man in his late twenties. He kept bowing his head. Odds were this was the owner of the car being towed. He was likely telling the cop what had happened. But he seemed to be taking it in stride; presumably no one got hurt.

As Sakuta reached that conclusion, Mai said, “Looks like a solo crash.” She had her phone in her hand. “Seems like it happened at six. See?”

She showed him her phone. On-screen was a photo of the minivan slipping in the snow and striking the traffic sign. A passerby had grabbed the shot and posted it online. The post clearly said they hadn’t hit anyone.

When he saw the picture, Sakuta was seized by the oddest sensation. By the time he realized anything was amiss, he was already spinning out. It felt like every emotion was firing at once, kicking up massive waves in his heart. Unable to rein in his emotions, he couldn’t breathe and his chest was pounding.

A moment later he was hit by a terrible sense of loss. The agony was unbearable. When that passed, a wave of grief took its place, and it was all he could do to not to scream. He ground his teeth, enduring—and felt as if he heard a voice calling his name.

Sakuta!

But he didn’t know who. The voice echoed in his mind, but not his ears, and it soon faded.

“Sakuta?”

He looked up and saw Mai’s face through blurry vision. She seemed concerned. Mai was here. Mai was with him. Once he was sure of it, relief flooded him and his eyes started to sting. He tried to stop himself, but it was too late.

Without knowing why, he started shedding tears.

“Seriously, what’s gotten into you?”

She spoke in a gentle, soft voice. He could tell Mai was here, with him, and that made his tears feel warm.

The sudden flood of emotion vanished as abruptly as it had arrived. The pain, the sadness—all ebbed away and did not return.

All that was left was a feeling as warm as his tears. The desire to treasure the one he loved.

“Mai.”

The umbrella fell from his hand. Before it landed upside down on the ground, Sakuta said her name again and put his arms around her.

Just being able to say her name was a joyous thing.

Having Mai in his arms was a blessing.

This simple fact filled his heart to the brim.

“Ack, Sakuta, don’t!”

“……”

“I said wait until we get home.”

She was rebuking him, but her voice was soothing. She’d put her hands on his chest to resist, but without much force behind them. She was still concerned about his still unexplained waterworks.

He tried to speak, but no words came.

“……”

“……”

A brief silence.

“Sakuta?” She called his name. Just like she always did. But he knew this time it was checking to see if he was okay.

“……I’m fine.”

“Really?”

“I’m fine as long as I’m like this.”

He wasn’t sad. He wasn’t suffering. The tears had stopped, and his voice wasn’t quivering. His body was filling with warmth like sunlight. And that warmth came from Mai, wrapped in his arms.

“Well, fine, just this once.”

That reassurance made him tighten his grip.

Mai let him, giving herself over to his embrace.

After a while, he began to feel her pulse. He was sure she could feel his heartbeat, too. She’d let out a breath that tickled.

He wasn’t sure how long they stayed like that.

But when he next looked up, the cop car had left the intersection. The tow truck had hauled the crashed minivan away.

“Sakuta, pick up that umbrella. We’re getting snow on our heads.”

“I’m fine with that.”

“Don’t blame me if you catch a cold.”

“I can’t wait to have you look after me.”

“I’ll only be cooking for Kaede.”

“Can you feed me some canned tangerines?”

“If you can joke, then you must be all better.”

“Not yet!”

But even as he argued the point, there was a vibration at their hips. The steady rhythm was coming from Mai’s phone, in the pocket of her down coat. Someone was calling and not giving up.

“I bet that’s Nodoka.”

The death knell for their Christmas Eve.

“You don’t have to answer.”

“Nodoka would blow her top.”

But Mai didn’t reach for her phone. The ringing stopped after a while.

And soon started again. Very consistent, very insistent.

“See, Sakuta. Let go.”

The nagging vibrations finally peeled him off her.

Mai took out her phone, looked at the screen, and nodded.

“Mai, let me take it.”

Sakuta held out his hand, so Mai put her phone in it. Nodoka was on the incoming-call screen.

He accepted the call.

“The number you have called is not in service,” Sakuta said.

“Why are you answering?” she asked, clearly furious already. “Put my sister on!”

“Can’t.”

“Why not?”

“Mai’s busy brushing the snow off my head.”

When she was done with that, she moved on to his shoulders.

“Hah? Why are you making her do that? Why was there snow on you at all? Where are you, and what are you doing?”

“We’re having a delightful date.”

He picked up the umbrella and shook off the snow. He held it up and looked at Mai—but she’d already opened her own umbrella.

“I’ll be home soon, so your date’s over,” Nodoka said.

“Go have a post-show party with the girls.”

“The trains could stop at any moment, so we’re not sticking around.”

He heard a station announcement over the phone. She was waiting for a train that very second.

“I was hoping they’d have stopped already.”

“Then I’d take a cab.”

She was getting home tonight, come hell or high water.

“Well, be careful on your way home.”

“Huh? What’s that for?”

“Message from Mai,” he lied.

“Your date’s done, so get on home, Sakuta.”

“Don’t rush me. They’ve still got half-priced cakes left.”

“Who cares about that!”

“So you don’t want any?”

“I’ll take cake if you’ve got it, but—Augh, that’s my train. I’ll be home by nine!”

“Got it. I’ll flirt with Mai till then.”

“Don’t you dare!”

With that, she hung up.

He handed the silent phone back to Mai.

“What did Nodoka say?”

“I’m supposed to flirt with you until nine.”

“Don’t lie.”

She smiled and pocketed her phone.

“Let’s grab a cake and head on home.”

Her hand touched his, fingers locking with his—then she pulled him along.

He walked with her.

“Mai,” Sakuta said, calling the name of the girl he loved.

“Mm?” She gave him a curious look.

“……”

He searched for the words but didn’t have a name for the warmth living inside him. So like a total fool, he just called her name again.

“Mai.”

“Yes, what?” She giggled.

And that smile made him feel even warmer.

There was lots he didn’t understand, and he was still convinced he’d forgotten something vital. But he was sure that was okay for now.

He was so close to Mai’s smile.

He could feel her warmth through their clasped hands.

It was an ordinary day, spent with the one who mattered most to him.

And as long as he knew that, he’d be okay.

As long as he remembered that, he could find this warmth again.

And one day, he’d get where he was meant to go.
